subsubtopic: SALE OF CANDU REACTOR TO SOUTH KOREA-POSSIBLE SUSPENSION OF SALE-ARRANGEMENTS TO ASSURE PEACEFUL USE OF NUCLEAR MATERIAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who yesterday indicated that the political and military situation in South Korea today did not warrant a change in the position of the government with regard to the sale of the CANDU reactor. In the face of growing concern about possible renewed military conflict in Korea, is the government prepared to suspend the CANDU sale independently of what kind of assurances can be negotiated on a bilateral basis?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SALE OF CANDU REACTOR TO SOUTH KOREA-POSSIBLE SUSPENSION OF SALE-ARRANGEMENTS TO ASSURE PEACEFUL USE OF NUCLEAR MATERIAL
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: SALE OF CANDU REACTOR TO SOUTH KOREA-POSSIBLE SUSPENSION OF SALE-ARRANGEMENTS TO ASSURE PEACEFUL USE OF NUCLEAR MATERIAL
speechtext: Will the minister tell the House just what safeguards the government is proposing to South Korea, and will he admit that while arrangements may be made which will provide adequate inspection, these arrangements will provide no means of preventing South Korea from using, for non-peaceful purposes, plutonium and techniques provided by Canada?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SALE OF CANDU REACTOR TO SOUTH KOREA-POSSIBLE SUSPENSION OF SALE-ARRANGEMENTS TO ASSURE PEACEFUL USE OF NUCLEAR MATERIAL
speechtext:
As I mentioned yesterday, the safeguards which are provided for in the case of South Korea, in a sense, fall into two categories. The ratification of the non-proliferation Treaty by South Korea which stipulates that the total nuclear system of the country will be subjected to international inspection under the international agency. Second, we are negotiating a bilateral agreement with South Korea putting into effect the total range of safeguards which were announced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, I believe, last December 20. This is the most complete possible range of safeguards available at the present time. The diversion of plutonium or material for non-peaceful purposes is, of course, subject to the examination and inspection system of the international agency, and I am sure it is clear to the Leader of the Opposition that if that occurred, it would be instantly known to the international inspectors.
Obviously a new situation would be created at that point in which the international community would be alerted to this diversion which might be taking place. That is about the best answer I can give to the hon. member, and in reply to the hon. member for Calgary North, it is the best the international community has devised up to the present time. Perhaps the hon. member will be able to improve it at a later date.

I put it to the Prime Minister, in light of what took place in India and in light of the moral responsibility that any government has in a field like this, is the government of Canada prepared to proceed with the sale of CANDU reactors in these circumstances with no way of preventing the use of such techniques and plutonium for non-peaceful purposes? Mr. Chairman, having heeded the Prime Minister's admonition of this past Monday to read Machiavelli, I should like to begin today's debate with a quote from that source as follows:
There is nothing more true than that if there are no soldiers where there are men it is not owing to any natural or local defect but is solely the fault of the prince.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Let us remember this, for indeed the current state of affairs which finds the forces undermanned, overtasked, ill-directed and armed with obsolete equipment is the result of a decade of neglect by the government. Given neither thoughtful direction by cabinet nor the resources needed to maintain an effective, modern force, the Department of National Defence has been allowed to drift to its present state of near chaos.
Canada is not a militarist state. We do not seek to be awesome and feared. Yet an ability to defend one's sovereignty and to fulfil one's international obligations is necessary: it is a prerequisite for even a "just society". Perhaps the Prime Minister would prefer this to be couched in the terms of the classics, and for this I turn once more to Machiavelli, who said:
Neither abundance of money nor natural strength of the country will suffice, nor will the loyalty and goodwill of his subjects endure. For these cannot remain faithful to a prince who is incapable of defending them. Neither mountains nor lakes nor inaccessible places will present any difficulties to an enemy where there is a lack of brave defenders.
It is tempting, Mr. Chairman, to discuss once again some of the specific problems which plague the armed forces; indeed, such an exposition could be continued for days. However, I will instead discuss broader policy questions for I was particularly struck by a statement which the Prime Minister is reported to have made-a statement to the effect that democratic governments cannot expect the people they represent to support defence policies automatically and without question, and that a continuous challenging of tactics and strategies was necessary for the government to be convinced of their worth and, in turn, for it to be able to convince parliament and the people of the worth of those policies.
It was, therefore, with some eagerness that I awaited the Prime Minister's statement on the NATO conference, for major changes are taking place and extremely important decisions are being made within the alliance. I thought he would perhaps outline the government's position and, at the very least, he would surely acquaint us with the issues

as he saw them and encourage a dialogue. I was to be disappointed. I use the words of the member for Oshawa-Whitby, who said:
On the question of NATO and the role Canada is to play in NATO, we got absolutely nothing from the Prime Minister.
Given that the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence are unwilling to discuss the current strategic and military situation internationally or within NATO, I feel that it is my duty to give the report that the Prime Minister should have given on Monday and raise this subject in the hope that it will provoke greater discussion of the decision which Canada must make soon with respect to its defence policy.
The past two years have brought great changes in the military situation in many areas of the world. The Yom Kippur war, the ensuing oil embargo and price rise, all have drastically altered the economic situation and consequently the military situation in the Middle East. The seemingly eternal war in Viet Nam seems now to be over. Cyprus has been invaded by Turkey, bringing Turkey and Greece to the brink of war. Finally, Portugal has begun to divest herself of African colonies. These events have not been without their internal causes and repercussions, but more of that later.
The diplomatic scene, too, has been far from quiet. The Strategic Arms Limitations Talks-SALT-have resulted in an initial agreement; the conference on security and co-operation in Europe seems about to produce some accords; talks between Arabs and Israelis continue sporadically. While the age of detente may seem to be upon us, let us not delude ourselves that the world is as we might wish it to be. Consider, for example, this assessment by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute:
SALT and certain other arms control measures have, of course, had very important, far reaching political consequences. In particular, they have significantly contributed to the improvement of relations between some states. But, in general, they have not produced any actual disarmament, nor have they even stopped the arms race.
There are two observations to be emphasized from this statement: firstly, we are in, and are likely to remain in, an era of a balance of terror, one of mutual assured destruction capabilities; secondly, the relations between states and their perceptions of each other's intentions are very important. On this latter point, let me give an example from the structure of forces in Europe. On the NATO side there is widespread concern over the very offensive disposition of the Warsaw Pact troops, a concern heightened by the latter's overwhelming superiority in armoured forces. On the other hand, the Warsaw Pact must be concerned with NATO's reliance on quick reaction aircraft as they are very vulnerable to a pre-emptive attack and, therefore, must be perceived as rather offensive weapons themselves. This intense interest with intentions and capabilities may seem abstract and academic, but in our nervous world it is, quite literally, of deadly importance.
Let us now turn for a moment to see just what the specific outcomes of the strategic agreements have been. The first meeting, the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks- SALT I-resulted in an interim agreement signed in 1972. Generally speaking, it froze the holdings of intercontinental missiles, but not warheads, at 1,054 for the United States and 1,618 for the U.S.S.R. The number of subma-

rine-launched ballistic missiles, or SLBMs, was likewise frozen at 656 for the United States and 740 for Russia. You will notice that Russia was higher in both cases. The SLBM levels were raised later, however, owing to an ongoing U.S.S.R. submarine building program, to 710 missiles on 44 submarines for the Americans and 950 missiles for the U.S.S.R., on 62 submarines.
In brief, the United States agreed to superior numbers of heavier missiles for the Russians; this was because the United States held a technological lead in the production of multiple independently-targeted re-entry vehicles, or MIRVs, which in plain language means a missile with several warheads.
The next agreement was the Vladivostok agreement of last November. This new agreement limits each side to 2,400 missiles or heavy bombers, of which 1,320 can carry MIRVs. It is my feeling that the Vladivostok agreement, while it sets numerical ceilings on the strategic arms levels, has several serious faults: first, the restriction is on numbers and not on qualitative developments; second, the limits are too high by far. Moreover, many major problems were ignored: for example, the identification of MIRV missiles cannot be done with current surveillance methods. No one will be able to tell whether any country has exceeded the limit of their MIRV missiles. Finally, the omission of the Russian "backfire" bomber, cruise missiles, strike aircraft, bomber standoff missiles and IRBMs from the list indicates how much further the negotiations must go.
Due to the lack of a qualitative ceiling, the Russians are at present flight testing four new missiles. The U.S.S.R. has always had an advantage in weight per missile, and it is estimated that if the new missiles are all deployed the U.S.S.R. would have a "throw weight" advantage of five or six to one; that is, ten million to twelve million pounds for the Russians to two million pounds for the United States. This possible imbalance caused President Ford to indicate that they might try to develop a new rocket motor technology in an attempt to catch up.
I believe that civilization's best chance for survival is for these two superpowers to remain fairly equally balanced militarily. In the short term and over the intermediate term perhaps we can talk them down from the over-arming of the recent past. The limitations imposed by SALT I and Vladivostok are, at best, only a start.
Turning from the global strategic situation, let us now look at the European theatre and in particular at the political pressures within NATO. Over the course of the past few years the relations between NATO states have shifted dramatically. The most obvious example is that of Turkey and Greece; set off by the events on Cyprus and fueled by disagreement in the Aegean, the discord between the two has reached a point where it threatens the very existence of NATO's so-called "southern flank".
There has also arisen a basic difference in attitude between the United States and France. President Giscard seeks to be a bridgebuilder between industrialized, oil consuming Europe and the OPEC group as well as other third world producers. President Ford, in contrast, has sought a common front of industrialized oil consumers to
June 5, 1975

exert joint pressures on the producers. In this pursuit, the Americans have tended to see NATO as an economic as well as a military alliance that should strengthen the western position.
Tensions and uncertainties have also arisen because of changes within certain countries. Perhaps the most important changes are being made within the United States where, occasioned by the collapse of the South Vietnamese regime, a reassessment and debate on basic external policy issues seems to be starting. This debate will certainly be important to NATO simply because of the predominant role which the U.S. plays in the alliance.
Forced to do so by her economic plight, Britain has decided upon a substantial reduction in her armed forces and on a withdrawal from the Mediterranean. This will, like the Turkey-Greece dispute, seriously affect the southern flank, although a recent Italian decision to strengthen her navy may offset the British action to some degree.
Finally, and again on the southern flank, there is Portugal. After decades under a right-wing dictatorship, the majority of the Portuguese people are now trying to establish a functioning democracy. We who have been blessed with democracy for a century-I consider that 1867 to 1975 is more than a century-may not realize how difficult this is. There is the very real possibility that the attempt at democracy will fail and end in left-wing dictatorship. This would be tragic, just as a lapse back to right-wing dictatorship would be tragic.
I was pleased to see that the government has invited a Portuguese mission to Ottawa to discuss bilateral trade arrangements. Anything which Canada can do to strengthen the democratic forces in Portugal is to the good. While in narrow military terms the changes in Portugal add uncertainty to the NATO picture, we must accept this and try to show to the Portuguese people that NATO can be a beneficial economic as well as military organization and that it encourages democracy. In summing up the Portuguese situation, I will quote from an editorial in the Edmonton Journal: It says:
Let Portugal sort out her own internal affairs and work out her own destiny. NATO will be better off with a healthy relationship with whatever new Portugal emerges from the present upheavals, than tied to the forces of reaction and repression that have inevitably provoked their own unpopularity and downfall.
With the conclusion of this brief examination of some of the recent political trends in NATO, I will now turn, Mr. Chairman, to more direct military questions. Just at the time when the developments on the southern flank threaten the viability of NATO as a regional alliance, an unprecedented and particularly worrisome disparity in armoured strength has developed between NATO and the Warsaw Pact countries. According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, while the figures for northern and central Europe are, NATO 620,000 troops versus Warsaw Pact 910,000, in main battle tanks the figures are, NATO 7,000 versus Warsaw Pact 20,000.
It has been the custom over the past three decades to console ourselves in the face of these odds by remembering the nuclear deterrent; that is, if the U.S.S.R. attacked our numerically inferior forces on the ground in western Europe, then we would use tactical nuclear battlefield weapons. This has always seemed to me to be a very
Business of Supply
unsatisfactory answer. I have never been able to convince myself that the use of atomic weapons can be restricted to narrow military battlefields. While the first nuclear weapon might be used on a troop concentration, the next one is as likely to be used on a staging area, and so on, until within hours Washington and Moscow are targets and the holocaust is upon us.
I am certain that I have not been alone in my concern about the practicality or sanity of the atomic deterrent being our only deterrent in western Europe. We have seen NATO progress from the original "trip-wire" theory to the "flexible response", and to "selective targeting" where the targets would be military installations rather than cities. This is supposed to give the President of the United States a broader range of options than existed previously, provided of course that he is still around after the other side exercises its option.
The use of battlefield nuclear weapons has become an important issue of debate within NATO itself. Senator Nunn's amendment in the U.S. Senate requested the U.S. department of defence to examine and justify the 7,000 nuclear warheads in western Europe-the U.S.S.R. in comparison, is thought to have between 3,500 and 7,000. The basic quandary remains unchanged, however. A strong deterrent position on the part of the United States gives their NATO allies a false sense of security and they immediately react by reducing their conventional forces. On the other hand, any evident lack of resolve to use the deterrent encourages the only possible enemy and arouses European fears that the strategic support of the United States would evaporate under the pressure of all-out nuclear confrontation.
Mr. Schlesinger is a strong supporter of "essential equivalence." He has pointed out:
Deterrence is not a substitute for defence: defensive capabilities, representing the potential for offensive counteraction are the essential conditions of deterrence. This simple truth becomes especially evident in a crisis, when forces designed only for "deterrence" are increasingly found to be lacking in credibility both to opponents and to potential users.
This question of the credibility of the deterrence is crucial. As long as we rely solely upon a nuclear deterrent, any aggressor whose objectives are limited can delude himself that his aggression will not provoke a nuclear response. A capability for a balanced and suitable reaction to a wide range of situations is the keystone of any reasonable defence policy.
Given that an effective NATO capable of responding to many different situations is a necessary part of western European stability and, hence, of Canadian security, two questions should be asked of the Canadian involvement. First, are we doing our share in NATO? Second, is the money Canada is spending being used wisely? Our share in NATO, it would seem to a fairminded person, should be based on our resources and our ability to commit them. On examination one finds that our military budget, based on percentage of our GNP, comes in twelfth out of 13, being ahead of tiny Luxembourg only. We are seen to be a wealthy nation acting as the cheapest skate in NATO.
As for the wisdom with which the money is spent, NATO as a whole leaves much to be desired in the way of economic husbanding of funds. A recent study commis-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the hon. member for Victoria for bringing before this House the subject of defence, a subject which is not particularly popular with the press or with the general public. Yet no one who thinks about the subject can doubt its importance. Our sovereignty depends upon our defence. The maintenance of a stable world and stable peace depends upon methods of defence such as peacekeeping. The economic consequence of an expenditure of more than $2 billion a year of our budget makes it a subject that we have an obligation to consider.
I am afraid that what I am going to say will not very much interest the Minister of National Defence. I am going to discuss a subject which I have previously discussed with him and the House. I do not think the minister will find very much that is new. I believe the major decision that has been made in the field of defence is a wrong decision. I refer to the decision to renew the agreement known as NORAD. I know that the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence has made a majority report recommending such action. I want to take this opportunity to say that a minority of that com-

mittee, and I do not know whether it consisted of other than myself and the hon. member for New Westminster-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: And the hon. member for Fraser Valley West.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
The three of us had a different view. I shall briefly try to state that view. We thought the result of the recommendation should be that our government should confer at an early date with the government of the United States, with a view to working out a new, effective means of co-operation in the fields of early warning, detection, surveillance and, where necessary, interception with regard to any invasions of North American air space.
I want to point out again to this House that the stated purpose of NORAD has long been obsolete. That stated purpose was defence against the manned bomber. Although there is lip service paid from time to time, including the majority report of the committee and the minister's statements, to the diminishing, de-emphasized, reduced threat of manned bombers, we continue to say that although that is no longer the principal objective of NORAD it is, in a somewhat reduced form, one of the major objectives. When speaking to the committee on February 27, the minister said:
The first factor to be considered is the bomber threat.
He went on to say that as the Soviet Union has built up its strategic missile forces, the relative importance of manned bombers has continued to decline. The Soviet Union, nonetheless, continues to maintain a sizeable force of longrange bombers, and as long as it does he believes the security interests of this country necessitate our continuing this defence against manned bombers. I am not quoting the minister exactly. Precisely the same view was expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. While he admitted that the bomber threat was of a lesser degree than the missile threat, he still thought that Canada should co-operate with the United States in the maintenance of some form of defence against the bomber threat.
In our view, the time has come to bury this hoary myth and fallacy once and for all, clearly and unequivocally. There is no longer a realistic threat of the use of Soviet bombers in an all-out attack on North America. Expert opinion, common sense and the actions of the U.S.S.R. confirm this opinion. In 1968, the then United States Secretary of Defence, Mr. McNamara, was asked this question in a committee of the Senate, by Senator Miller:
Looking down the road, is it not feasible that they-
That is referring to the U.S.S.R.
-might have as an option the use of selective targets with their bombers and no resort to missiles at least in the early stages of the war?
Secretary McNamara replied:
Completely inconceivable, I think. The reason is that by launching these bombers against our warning systems, they would give us the opportunity to retaliate before they hit us.
I wish to put on record a more recent quotation from James Schlesinger, the United States Secretary , of Defence. I am not quoting obscure, theoretical men, but the people responsible for the defence of North America as
June 5, 1975

a whole under the treaty, and certainly of the United States. He said, in 1974:
Without an effective anti-missile defence precluded to both the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. by ABM (SALT) treaty of 1972, a defence against Soviet bombers is of little practical value.
General Guy Simonds, formerly chief of staff in this country, when speaking to the defence committee of this House as long ago as 1964 said that the two or three hours warning of an impending manned bomber attack afforded by the early warning and detection system eliminated the possibility of such an attack unless the Russians were crazy. He said they clearly were not crazy then, and they are not crazy now. Those who continue to speak of the continuing, albeit diminishing threat of a manned bomber attack on North America-as the committee report does, and the minister from time to time-refuse to assess the continued reality of such a threat. They refuse to attribute any degree of rationality to their opponents. Their refusal to meet this argument head-on suggests that it is unanswerable. As a last resort, they state that reality of the threat of the bombers rests in the fact that the U.S.S.R. has continued to maintain some 140 aging intercontinental bombers. It has not increased the number and did not even at the time it was substantially expanding its missiles armoury.
In the Vladivostok understanding arising out of the SALT agreement, the two great nuclear powers set a limit on their delivery systems for nuclear weapons. They included both missiles and manned bombers within the limit. It seems absolutely clear that the U.S.S.R. has no intention of embarking once again on an expanded international manned bomber program. The minister might ask why, then, the U.S.S.R. continues to maintain the present stock of manned bombers. The answer seems to have been given to our committee by Professor David Cox of Queen's University, and I quote:
It is equally plausible for the Soviet Union to take the view that by maintaining a bomber force at however low level a capacity, they can also force the United States and Canada to maintain anti-bomber defences at a much greater rate of financial attrition.
In other words, they maintain them to induce us to continue what we have been doing without any sense for years, that is, maintain under NORAD a substantial means of meeting a threat they would not carry out, as General Simonds said, unless they were crazy. I suggest the survival of the theory of defence against a manned bomber threat is not just a matter of academic interest; it justifies a mentality that diverts Canadian defence from its essential roles. The essence of a sound defence policy, particularly in an era of inflation and the diminishing value of the defence dollar, is to concentrate on essential roles and to provide effective means and equipment to combat real threats. We must discard the mentality that continues to meet threats which, if they ever were real, have long since become obsolete.
I think the real choice before the committee and before the government was, not whether we should renew NORAD or completely repudiate co-operation in defence matters, especially affecting air space, with the United States but whether a better approach might have been to say to the United States: We face a new situation. The
Business of Supply
main purpose of the old treaty has disappeared. We want to negotiate new means of dealing with the threat to our common air space. We no longer believe that joint control is an essential part of these arrangements and we want to see whether we can operate these things on our own with an exchange of information and quite possibly an exchange of weapons. We think that would be a better way of handling this situation.
However, it appears the minister did not even address his mind to this alternative. For him, it was NORAD or nothing. He closed his mind to the alternative which was available, a new arrangement of a different type. He did not ask his staff or his military advisers about it; he told us so in committee. He did not discuss this matter with the United States. Mr. Chairman, we have never questioned the proposition that we should co-operate with the United States in many of these areas. What was questioned was whether we should continue this particular form of cooperation when in our view it is no longer necessary.
The main argument used by the Minister of National Defence and by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in favour of the continuation of NORAD was that to do so was essential to satisfactory relations with the United States. We pressed the minister on this contention. We asked him who told him that this was the case. He could think of nothing but vague conversations a long time ago with Mr. Schlesinger.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs assured us that the United States wanted this agreement continued. When we pressed him for reasons, conversations, letters, articles or anything which showed this view to have substance, we drew a complete blank. So the main argument in favour of the renewal of NORAD, the impact or the alleged impact of non-renewal on Canadian-United States relations, was not supported by evidence and the government's automatic willingness to accept the renewal of NORAD without question is an example of mental subservience, an example of the lack of an independent will to make decisions for ourselves.
Given the view which I believe most people share- though not all, I admit-that the NORAD agreement is no longer of military value, why must we defer to the possibly imaginary view that failure to renew it might irritate the United States? The sovereignty of our air space is important and it should not lightly be sacrificed. But even more important is independence of thought in policy-making. This is a basic element of sovereignty and independence. The government tells us from time to time, in foreign policy papers and elsewhere, that this is one of the goals of Canadian foreign policy.
Sometimes we hear talk about the cost element in any new arrangement. We are told it would cost much more to "go it alone" in defending our sovereignty than if there were a joint agreement with the United States. This view is based upon the simplistic reasoning that we would need to duplicate everything that has been done under NORAD before any new approach could be successful. I refer to the defence of our sovereignty, the surveillance of our air space, measures against interception, and so on. As far as I know, the minister and others speaking for him have totally failed to indicate precisely what is necessary in these areas.

June 5, 1975
Business of Supply
After all, we are not trying to defend ourselves militarily against aggression from the United States, even if we feared it. What sort of attack on our sovereignty do we expect? What are the weapons required to deal with such an attack? What would they cost? If this information were given us in a clear form, we might be able to arrive at a sensible answer to these questions. I should like the minister to tell us at some stage in this debate just what is required in this so-called surveillance role. It could be an unlimited commitment or it could be a limited, rational commitment which will meet our needs.
The renewal of the NORAD agreement was said by some to be a justified symbol of good relations between Canada and the United States. My view is that failure to renew NORAD would have been viewed by many people as a symbol of Canadian determination and Canadian sovereignty and it would have been not inconsistent with the closest co-operation between ourselves and the United States. I am glad, however, that the committee and the minister did move some way from arguments in justification of NORAD which have made no sense in the past.
I see I have a minute or two in which to discuss NATO. Here again, we are left in limbo. The Prime Minister came back last Tuesday, I think it was, and made a statement to the House that we would continue our support of NATO and we would not diminish our military contribution. But since he added that some review was in progress, he left the nature of that contribution wide open. Shall we be contributing to the central force, which will require us to buy a whole lot of new tanks, for instance, if ground warfare is contemplated, or new aircraft, as the case may be? Or would it not be better for us to contribute a light, mobile force to be available on the flanks? It is on the flanks that the experts seem to think NATO is most vulnerable. I cannot imagine why we should continue a role inappropriate to our defence capability and means, a role which involves us in extraordinarily heavy expenditures.
I conclude by saying that when this defence structure review, as it is called, becomes available, I hope the minister will ensure that it is sent in good time, before it is finally accepted, to the committee on defence. I am tired of finding that decisions have been made and announced-as was the case in the decision respecting NORAD-before these matters are referred to the committee. "You can look into it if you like", they tell us; but we all know what the answer will be in circumstances of that kind.
The hon. member for Victoria mentioned Portugal. I have had the good fortune to be in Portugal, and I take this opportunity of expressing my conviction of the democratic concern of the people of Portugal. I believe they are willing to co-operate with the western world in any reasonable way that is required. I think the talk we have heard about communist takeovers, and so on, is completely without foundation and I hope it will never be a basis for our policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that the choice made by the Progressive Conservative party and the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) to discuss

the estimates of the Department of National Defence is one which meets the approval of the House. We have rarely, I think, had a discussion on this subject in the committee of the whole in recent years.
These estimates have of course been discussed in committee, but we had got out of the habit of debating them in the committee of the whole, and the new procedure allows us to discuss the estimates of a department, those estimates we feel are the most important. Yet our discussion of the problems of this department this afternoon has shown us that there is something to be said about both sides.
Having heard the speech made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), I wonder what Canada would become if the country was run by his party. Perhaps there would be some savings in national defence, but I wonder if those savings would be worthwhile in the short or long run. Yet, Mr. Chairman, we know that any country wishing to have its sovereignty respected must have an army, even a token one. In the present situation, judging by the way roles are played in the world, we have witnessed for some decades the establishment of blocs on both sides. It is a well known fact that every country's military expenses take a large part of governmental budgets. It has practically become inevitable.
We know it is a very costly proposition for a country like Canada which has vast boundaries to defend and a population of barely 22 million inhabitants. Maintaining adequate defence forces is quite an expense.
In the last few years, we have seen the government, mainly in response to pressures from the Canadian public, try to limit its defence budget, with the result we see today. By restricting expenditures, replacement of obsolete equipment has been neglected. Now, today, we are faced with the situation where land equipment, some trucks, are older than the troops that drive them. A few years ago, I visited a military base and saw trucks burning out their fourth engine. At that point, drivers hesitate to venture any distance from camp, for fear they might have to walk back.
Mr. Chairman, when a situation reaches that point, one can have qualified troops, well trained troops, but I wonder how we could defend ourselves with such equipment if we really had to use it one day.
The same applies to heavy artillary. And what about our planes? Our maritime patrol and search planes such as the Argus are already obsolete, and we are told it would cost some $400 to $700 million to replace them.
Of course, this will not be in this year's nor in next year's; I imagine the amount will have to be spread over several years. On the other hand, if we want to go on patrolling our coastline, we will have to provide for the replacement of this plane and for the amounts required in the estimates of the Department of National Defence.
Our fighters are also very old, and we wonder if they would still be effective in case of conflict. They can still be used to train our pilots but, then again, they train on planes which are easy to handle, it is true, but sometimes they must use blank ammunition for their training.
In that sense, our soldiers also complain about not having the necessary equipment to complete their training
June 5, 1975

adequately. Mr. Chairman, generally we have to support the enemy or opponent with regard to the maintenance of a defence army, a well-equiped army. It is a known fact that at the Aeronautics Show in France, big manufacturers vie with one another in selling the most sophisticated aircrafts to NATO. Now if Canada lags behind, it will quickly be out distanced. Those are the facts that face us.
According to press reports today, the U.S.S.R. has just launched what is called a string of satellites. Indeed, they have put into orbit around the earth eight Cosmos satellites, probably for the purposes of setting up a world communication network for Soviet navy units. We also know how fast the USSR is building boats of all kinds, military or other, which are sent to sea all over the world, and I do not think they are playing that game for the tourist trade.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as long as Russia will keep in action and develop a conventional striking force, we shall have to take the same means to defend ourselves. If the Warsaw Pact bloc had only nuclear weapons, NORAD and NATO could also have an all-nuclear defence. But as long as the Warsaw Pact nations, led by Russia, will maintain, for instance, conventional bombers-and we know that it still has the most sophisticated long-range bombers-we never know when Russia will use them to launch a conventional attack on the North American continent or elsewhere. So, as long as Russia will maintain that kind of weapons, I think we must do the same.
Given these facts, the problem is this: Since on the communist side, be it Russia or its satellites, when they need funds to make weapons, they do not care much about what the Russians, the Poles, the Turks or the Hungarians think, they just go ahead. If they have to call in engineers and technicians, to use the smelting works and the plants to manufacture these war weapons, they do, whereas on the side of democracies it is not the same thing, not the same tune.
If the Canadian government, for instance, makes any mention of increasing its national defence budget, cries are heard throughout Canada. Newspapers get hold of the story, especially those that support the kind of speech heard before mine and want Canada and the United States, or any other country, to get rid of their armies. I wonder why. They probably know why, but if we were to do that, we would probably be in difficulty. There lies the question. Must we restrain our military expenses, or must we equip ourselves with arms, or with what I would call good quality tools, capable of being used by our servicemen? Such is the choice we are faced with.
Another very important point must also be brought out. Notwithstanding the nature or size of the national defence budget, be it at the top, or in fourth, fifth or sixth position in the overall Canadian budget, everyone knows there is always some waste. That seems anchored in the minds of our citizens, of our industrialists, of our businessmen and even of our civil servants. When it comes to spending for national defence, there is no hesitating. There are no reduced costs. It seems that such a business has no competition. Full prices are charged, and no thought is given to any reduction, because there is no competition; on the contrary, prices are inflated. It is mostly with that in mind that I want to draw the minister's attention, and I ask him
Business of Supply
to be very careful, to make several checks and to be demanding towards all officials and divisions of his department, in order to prevent that wasting we are aware of, especially during certain periods.
Mr. Chairman, I would not like anyone to say I favour undue expenditures for defence. Neither would I like our defence system to be in danger and within easy grasp by just about anybody. That is, I think, the target every Canadian should have when dealing with expenditures and estimates in a democratic country.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity given us by the Conservative Party and the first speaker of that party, the hon. member for Victoria, to speak on the subject of defence. I agree to a certain extent with the suggestion that perhaps here in Canada defence is not a popular subject. There are reasons for this. I am sure there are other activities in our lives that would not win popularity contests. But if you spoke to the people of France, Germany, Poland or Russia you would find that defence is a popular subject. Perhaps it is not popular here because those of us with the experience of living through the second world war and the Korean war are in a minority today.
Canadians do not have a strong instinct to protect themselves from wars. That is why it is much more difficult for us to sell the idea of defence in Canada than it is in France, Germany or Britain where the people have experienced war once, and some even twice. To them defence is a very vivid and popular subject.

Most of all Mr. Chairman, I want to seize this opportunity to join others who have already paid homage to the members of the Canadian armed forces and I welcome this new opportunity to do so. I indicated earlier that I also served in the Canadian armed forces, as several of my colleagues. But we are now a minority which does not belong to the medium age group of members of the House of Commons or the Senate.
Indeed, we are a minority in two different ways, only, the Canadian armed forces have for very many years, surely since the 40's and even before, greatly contributed in building Canada's and the Canadians' reputation. They are a Canadian presence in Europe as well and in Egypt and elsewhere. Every time the Canadian armed forces were called to serve or help, they performed with the greatest distinction. To refer to statements often made about the members of the Canadian army, I should like for instance to recall what NATO Secretary General Joseph Luns sais following a tour of our armed forces in Europe. He mentioned how himself and the council members were impressed by the ability and competence of Canadian troops, also the excellent condition of their equipment and their typical flexibility in combining with our allies's forces.
I heard similar comments, Mr. Chairman, during the symposium on defence which I attended last February. The ministers of defence and the parliamentary delegates who attended were constantly repeating how the members of the Canadian armed forces had distinguished them-

selves by their abilities, their merits, their eagerness in their profession and their devotion.
I do not wish to deal more particularly with this issue, but it is the first opportunity given to me to recall also how valuable for the Canadian people of my province in 1970 was the support of the excellent members of the Canadian armed forces.
You have seen the films which are being distributed throughout the world showing the reactions in Canada and in Quebec to the 1970 events. Most of those who distribute those films are criticized, the government and those who took that decision. Surely this is because they were not witnesses. Those who make that insidious propaganda did not witness what happened in 1970. After the event, it is indeed very easy to claim that we had overestimated the gravity of the situation. It is like the manager of a baseball club who must decide whether the runner should try to steal home. When the play fails, 15,000 spectators can stand up and say: "Well, I could have told him that it would fail". In retrospective it is very easy to express an opinion and criticize the decision taken.
However, when we refer to the situation as it existed in October 1970, very few people, as far as I know, came forward voluntarily to give information as to the number of revolutionaries and their intention. I suggest that all those who criticize the government should say so. If someone had the information, why did he not reveal that this small group of hot heads wanted only to call the attention of the world on a situation which existed in the minds of a few people who have hang ups and who are living in a very special kind of anguish. There were a few enlightened people who could have informed us at the end of September or in early October and who ventured, came forward and volunteered information, saying it was a small group. And thanks to the federal government's action, and especially that of the Canadian Armed Forces, members of the armed forces very ably performed that awkward work. And I am referring here especially to the Canadian Armed Forces members who did not speak French and who were on duty in the province of Quebec facing the problems I just mentioned.
Therefore there were no regrettable incidents and those people deserve our congratulations, and against the whole world, those who are trying to spread false impressions as to what happened in the province of Quebec are making a mistake. I can say that as I lived through it and in a much more intense way, Mr. Chairman. One may recall that it was at the time of my election campaign to replace my predecessor, the Hon. Leo Cadieux, who was then Minister of National Defence. Therefore being a candidate in a federal election during September and October 1970, travelling through a constituency where people were known for hiding revolutionaries, one can be sure that I have a good idea of what happened and I am convinced that the Canadian government did not overreact to the situation existing then.
But those are not the remarks I wished to make, Mr. Chairman. What I wished to point out mainly is the Canadian troops' participation in NATO and also in NORAD. My colleague from Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) recalled the renewal of the NORAD agreement with our neighbours to the south. Others will surely want to deal

with that particular aspect of national defence activities. As for me, I should like to say a few words on NATO and point out that as much as the Marshall Plan was the cornerstone of the economic reconstruction in Europe after the war or immediately after, so did NATO contribute to ensure the military security that led to Europe's unification. And the role of NATO troops. The current situation in the world is such that it is absolutely essential to maintain some stability in Europe, a balance of forces between the two superpowers.
I do not mean here to question the intentions of the Soviets and the allies of member countries of the Warsaw Pack vis-a-vis western Europe; but we know the policy, and it is not a mere question of morality or good intentions. I feel there cannot be true, peaceful security and co-existence in the most positive sense without some equality of military forces, or-and it is utopia to think about it-total disarmament.
We have the responsibility to make sure with our European allies that any attempt to score by a surprise attack in Europe or America is checked by the second strike- that of response. So, if by that strike, that threat, the second strike, we eliminate any possibility of war, then we are maintaining a deterrent force that checks those who would have any intentions of attacking Europe and North America.
And it is that equality of forces that must be absolutely maintained, and on the basis of the information we have on purchases of equipment by member countries of the Warsaw Pact, equipment that is being built, the striking power of that equipment, the size and the number of the troops stationed in central Europe, it is absolutely unthinkable to consider the possibility of withdrawing from the commitment made with our allies and it is absolutely essential that NATO participation be maintained. Such was the intention of the right hon. Prime Minister when he went to Brussels recently. He stated unequivocally that Canada intended to remain present and active within the NATO alliance, and did not intend to reduce the effectiveness of its contribution.
I will give you my interpretation of what in my opinion the Prime Minister meant, and I will also tell you how I would imagine the Canadian contribution in Europe. I believe our Prime Minister first wanted to reassure our allies and those who criticised the Canadian participation. I do not think the expression "part-time partners" of NATO was an allusion to us. But our "unobstrusiveness" in Europe has often been criticized. Of course, when considering the distribution of troops, you realize that we have an important air force. Although I do not want to minimize the importance of the air force-which I belonged to in 1942, 1943, 1944 and 1945-1 think that if we are to reassess the contribution of Canada in the light of the recent statements of the Prime Minister, our first aim, considering the vast territory under our care, should be to protect that vast territory whose sovereignty is to be upheld. Maybe the activities and efforts of the air force should be maintained precisely to protect our country, supervise our land, and also meet the engagements we are about to enter into under an agreement which is expected to be signed very soon with respect to the limits of the
June 5, 1975

territory which will be placed under our surveillance on the eastern, northern and western coasts of Canada.
In view of this responsibility, of that vast tract of territory that we have to control and protect, given the changes brought about in the NORAD agreement so that the surveillance of the western sector of Canada be assured exclusively by Canadian forces, I believe that we should rather seriously think of limiting our participation in Europe to land forces, which would require less investment and could be achieved by an increase in our forces and in our visibility in terms of equipment, movement and also in terms of Canadian presence. We know that there are no fewer than 16,000 or 18,000 Canadians now living in West Germany. That figure might be increased.
Thus we could contribute to the acknowledgment of the fact that Canada already belongs to the European community. If it is true militarily speaking, if we are a member of the European military community, there only one step more to convince our allies that we should also be part of the economic, political and social community. I believe that a greater presence of Canadians in Europe could largely contribute to the achievement of that purpose. There is also the matter of the rationalization of equipment. In a symposium which took place in Munich last February, we dealt at great length with the use of the dollar that every country must spend for its defence. We know quite well that it is not easier here than it is in Europe to convince taxpayers that an important part of the budget must be devoted to defence. Here this share amounts to 10 per cent in England, it is 14 per cent. In France it is more for the reasons I mentioned earlier.
If only Canadians could be convinced of all the advantages that an intense presence in Europe can represent! We do not have to give lengthy explanations, for I think that Canadians can understand as well as we do the advantages of such a campaign to convince people that we are already part of the political and military community of Europe, why not make the last step and join the economic community?
As for equipment it might be visible but less expensive. The possibility has been and will be considered, hopefully not for too long, of repeating Israel's experience and modernizing our existing tanks. I am told the upgrading of one tank, the Centurion type, with modern diesel engine and armament to our allies' standards, and with heavier track to carry the equipment, might cost from $200,000 to $250,000. With the number of tanks we already have, and considering that we would have to buy new units as replacement, the investment would be lighter than if we were to buy modern tanks, as the American type now selling between $500,000 and $600,000 apiece. We are assured by experts that an updated, modernized Centurion tank might very well meet central Europe's present needs.
For these reasons, I feel it is urgent that Canada's participation be converted to ground participation. Considering the intentions stated by defence ministers of many European countries at the symposium, where the accent was on equipment rationalization, I believe we will not experience too much difficulty convincing our allies of the importance for Canada to keep mainly our air activi-
Business of Supply
ties, for the reasons I already submitted, and develop ground activity expertise.
I am convinced that if we have a good case to put to our allies, if it is well put and if the members of the committee share my views on the direction that might be given to our participation in Europe, I believe this could contribute to promote both in the cabinet and among our allies the idea that the Canadian participation could very well be a land participation.
Mr. Chairman, those are the comments I wanted to make. There is often mention of reduction as concerns the cost of maintaining forces in Europe by our allies and by Canada. People often talk about reduction and I was astounded to find that the word reduction seems to have hypnotized people. There are some who have a strange conception or definition of the word reduction. If we look at what is going on around us, in my opinion, the word reduction is outdated. Let us look at what happened in Asia. People may condemn and judge our American neighbours for not having kept their word when they had made an official commitment to protect South Vietnam.
The word reduction was perhaps used excessively and we, who have responsibilities, may also have been hypnotized by this word. In my opinion, it was used abusively. I consider that reduction is a thing of the past. We should be much more careful and ensure that the events of last April and May in Asia will not have a domino effect, like some are saying, and that Africa and other countries will not suffer the consequences.
Mr. Chairman, those are the comments I wanted to make, and I am very happy to have been able to make some contribution in clarifying somewhat Canada's participation in the NATO forces.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I, along with other hon. members, wish to participate in this debate which is basically, in theory anyway, on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. It gives an opportunity to hon. members interested in defence to either question or to make statements on this very large subject. I share the general feeling not only of my colleague from Victoria who led off for the loyal opposition, but also my hon. friend from Greenwood with whom I quite often differ on specific points. Often he goes one way and I go the other. But that does not detract from his sincerity and conviction, even though I sometimes think there is a lot of wool wrapped around his arguments.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle. He is the very distinguished chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, and as such he is somewhat handicapped in advocating any views. That is why I found it most delightful to listen to some of his views on the overseas situation. I say without hesitation that I hope I do not have to eat those words if we ever find ourselves in confrontation on the hustings. I think he is a worthy successor of his very illustrious predecessor who I think was minister of defence back in 1968 and 1969 and has now gone on to greener pastures and larger challenges as the ambassador to France. I wish the Prime Minister had been

June 5, 1975
Business of Supply
in the chamber this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Labelle. I hope he will read the report of this debate in Hansard so that some of the very cogent thoughts of the hon. member for Labelle can somehow percolate through the inner crustation of the Prime Minister.
I do not intend to be too provocative this afternoon. After all, it is a day in June. We welcome on the floor of the House the new deputy minister of the Department of National Defence, with his minister. The minister has been before the committee many, many times. I am glad the hon. member for Victoria brought on this debate and I welcome the Minister of National Defence, for whom in a personal way I have great fondness and affection, though sometimes in a parliamentary sense we do differ.
I was most pleased when I picked up the paper, long before the Prime Minister returned from his trip overseas, to read what he said when he left Brussels last week at a press conference he held after the NATO summit meeting. He said something which I have been advocating to the Minister of National Defence since I have been involved in the committee, and that goes back several years. Actually, I was involved in the committee before the minister became Minister of National Defence.
There is a former minister of defence sitting in this House. Part of my story goes back to 1968 and 1969, because we have had five ministers of defence in eight years under this government. No wonder there are real problems and questions up in the air about the direction in which we are going and what our objectives are. I read with interest that the Prime Minister said, quite properly, that our democracy is quite different from the countries behind the Iron Curtain which have a monolithic approach to defence. In those countries the leaders or the chairmen of socialist republic committees do not have to worry about public opinion. Any massive contribution to defence or offence is made by a highly organized monolithic group and there is no necessity to inform and educate the public.
I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Labelle and the hon. member for Victoria that in peacetime defence is not the most popular subject. Even in wartime when there may be patriotism, marching bands and national fervor because of the instincts of self-preservation which are prevalent, it is only a necessary subject.
I sympathize with the Minister of National Defence today, as I have for some time even though I am getting quite cross with him. How can anyone in this world who reads newpapers think there is the blissful peace of Christmas lore or the goodwill on earth toward all men after what has just happened in Southeast Asia and the tinderbox of the Middle East?
It has never ceased to amaze me that some in this House wonder if we should support the North American Defence Agreement, NORAD, or whether we should stay in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, NATO. I am too young to have served in any theatre of war, but I was a cadet in one of the wars. It is the success of some of the defence pacts such as NORAD and NATO which gives members of parliament and the scribes and pundits out-

side this House the luxury of pontificating about whether we need a treaty or defence pact.
Look at the reality of the world today. Even though we would love to be able to say that we do not need to spend a dollar on defence, we know that is not possible in view of what is happening in Southeast Asia and what is going on in the Middle East, which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has just visited, or in Africa. We know the situation is not stable. There was the SEATO pact in Southeast Asia which did not stabilize the situation there. Because of decisions taken by North Atlantic countries in the late 1940s and 1950s, a former prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, once said of NATO that it was long overdue. The government had no conviction before that and no commitment to defence.
The Prime Minister has said that there should be, and has to be dialogue and debate with the Canadian public to get support for alliances. I was pleased to hear that. As the Minister of Defence knows, I have been trying to get him to go across this country and talk about defence. I do not mean just to the inner circles, to the messes and the base tours-which of course are necessary-but to go on the Canadian Club circuit, the Rotary Club circuit, and so on. He should be able to talk about defence in an intelligent way, recounting the dilemmas that confront him, without trespassing on the sacrosanct area of security. He could speak about the options that confront him although not, of course, about the recommendations that he makes to cabinet. I am not going to overstress the minister's role today, however.
There is an irony in the statement that the Prime Minister made in Brussels about how you need debate and dialogue with the people in a democracy in order to get support for any alliance. Since the first major overt act of the governement in 1968 when the NATO forces were cut in half, the Prime Minister has had nothing to say. I have looked very quickly through some of the research offices of this House to find when the Prime Minister next spoke on defence, in terms of a substantive contribution to any debate in this House or across the country, and I have yet to find anything. Granted, there was the NATO meeting here last year when he spoke in general terms, there was the Commonwealth conference in Singapore when he pledged allegiance to the Commonwealth, and at Brussels he said we were committed to the NATO concept. Obviously, on his tours of the capital, he has spoken the odd sentence about Canada's role and what our concept is in terms of defence. In terms of any meaningful debate or dialogue, however, there has been nothing.
Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman-I could make a speech on this, and some day I may in this chamber or outside-the paradox of this Prime Minister in so many areas of policy is almost beyond belief. If he really believed what he said in Brussels last week about informing, educating and dialoguing with the people, why is he absent when the question of defence is being discussed and such large areas of policy have to be defined? Almost every year since 1968-69 there has been a white paper on defence. The minister knows that those papers have been changed almost before the ink was dry. In the white papers of 1971, 1972, 1973 and 1974 there was a brand new physical formula for defence. Not a year goes by without an inflation
June 5, 1975

factor and the whole thing has to be checked and reworked. The forces in Canada and overseas have been crippled because of the new, dynamic formula that had been developed!
I am not pretending that there have not been semantic statements on defence. The priority which evidently the Prime Minister agreed to in 1968-69 was sovereignty first, NATO second, NORAD third and peacekeeping fourth. Those are the priorities set out in the white paper. Since 1968 there have been five ministers of defence who have had something to say about the subject in debate. There has only been one prime minister since 1968, however. In 1968-69 he made a statement in the House on the changing role of NATO, justifying the change and slicing in half our NATO commitment overseas at that time.
Perhaps the minister or his officials can confront me with a meaningful statement on defence which has been made by a minister in this House. I suggest meaningful statements have not been made; the Prime Minister has not seen fit to become involved in any dialogue on defence and that has made the role of the minister more difficult. I do not want to excuse the minister. Granted, we face economic difficulties; granted, we live in times of pseudo peace; granted, the Prime Minister says many contradictory things: nevertheless, the Canadian people are entitled to be told the government's position on defence. There should be some dialogue on defence, and the lack of dialogue has made the minister's position difficult.
The Minister of National Defence should not be content merely to react, merely to acquiesce in the restraints which have been placed upon him. He should go out to the people and carry the message. He should take a leaf from the book of other ministers and do as they did when they carried their message to the Canadian people. The people are entitled to know what the government's conception is of our role in NATO. The hon. member for Labelle was glad the Prime Minister said there is some commitment to NATO. But, Mr. Chairman, admirable though that sentiment may be, hon. members want to know the specific form of that commitment.
At the recent meeting of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, certain members asked the Minister of National Defence what he means by "level of commitment." For example, we want to know what it means in terms of aircraft, men, tanks, destroyers, and so on. Of course, the minister said, as his predecessors in office and the Prime Minister had said, "These things are under review." This reminds me of Alice in Wonderland. I think Alice asked the caterpillar what a word meant and the caterpillar said, "It means anything I want it to mean." Alice said, "Good gracious, what happens if two words mean the same thing?" The caterpillar answered, "If they mean the same thing, I pay double for them." That just about sums up what has been happening in this House and what happened last week before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. We asked the minister to define our commitment in a meaningful way; so far, we do not have an answer.
Believing that one should say in this House what one has raised in the press-although one is motivated by
Business of Supply
sentiments of rhetoric when writing in the press, which may be of advantage from a political standpoint-I say to the minister that in this country there is consternation arising from policy decisions the government has taken in the field of defence. That being so, I consider it the minister's duty to go across this country and tell the people of Canada what the government's point of view is, and to put that point of view across. Let him imitate the Minister of Finance.
For several months after the election, the Minister of Finance was invisible; he was like a shadow. He was everywhere, trying to explain how the economy works and trying to sell something which he called consensus, even though my leader had raised the subject during the election campaign. The Minister of Finance accepted speaking invitations. I say nothing as to how successful he was and how much wiser we are for all his effort to sell the illusive concept of consensus. Perhaps we know a little more about it today. I say nothing of what happened in the election campaign, because my leader, if you remember, was in favour of a consensus and of a 90-day period after which laws would be passed. No, I will not talk about election dishonesty which involves the Prime Minister.
I am talking about our defence commitment. I do not understand why the minister cannot come clean with the people of Canada and explain exactly what our commitment is. What are the various factors we must consider, apart from money? How many aircraft does the commitment involve, how big a force, what supply machinery, and so on? These factors need to be worked out and we should be aware of the results.
Let me ask another question. When will the government make up its mind on a replacement long-range patrol aircraft-LRPA? We have been asking this question for years and it has been under study for years. Away back on March 16 and 17, 1969, the then minister of national defence, Mr. Cadieux, said that the question of a replacement was being considered. Good heavens, it took us less time to fight and win the second world war, which lasted about 51/2 years, than it will take to find a replacement LRPA. After spending $14 million in trying to decide between two prime contractors for the long-range patrol aircraft, the minister injects the Phoenix proposal into our discussion but does not tell the Canadian people what this involves. How many departments will it involve? Will it involve Defence, Fisheries, the Department of the Environment? I see you are about to rise, Mr. Chairman, and I have hardly begun.
