subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, defence is an important subject. Since we are debating an opposition motion moved on an opposition day, I am disturbed to note that there are only nine members of the official opposition in the chamber. I expected to see more opposition members here. I am sorry the hon. member for Greenwood is no longer present because my comments on defence will centre mainly on the NORAD agreement. If the hon. member were here, I would say to him that unfortunately we live in an imperfect world. In a perfect world we would not need defence commitments, the NORAD agreement or NATO. Since we live in a world beset with dangers, it behooves the Government of Canada to take all necessary steps to protect the sovereignty of our land.
The hon. member for Greenwood discussed one aspect of NORAD, defence against Russian bombers. He contends that as that threat no longer exists, we should end our commitment under the NORAD agreement. I suggest the hon. member dealt with only one small aspect of that agreement. He singled out one aspect, said it no longer applies and suggested, in so many words, that we should throw the agreement in the garbage can, so to speak. I am afraid the hon. member was being one-sided because he referred to only one minor part of the agreement.
I wish to go into a bit of the history of the NORAD agreement and bring it up to date. The original NORAD agreement, signed in 1958 between Canada and the U.S.A., involved an extension of the air defence co-operation that had developed between the two countries since the end of the second world war. Hon. members will recall, I am sure, that during this period the world tensions arising out of the cold war and the continuing growth of an already formidable Soviet bomber force underlined a North American need for protection. It was not something that Canada and the United States dreamed up. They did not just decide it was good to sign a few agreements. There was a threat that existed in 1948 and in 1958 which Canada and the United States realized. Defence planners in both Canada and the United States were convinced that the only strategic threat to North America lay in the possibility of attack from manned Soviet nuclear bombers. That was some years ago.
The NORAD agreement, setting up an integrated command structure for American and Canadian air defence, was thus a natural outgrowth of the times. In simple terms, it established a co-operative defence against Soviet bombers and at the same time provided protection for the United States strategic air command, the western world's main cold war deterrent. The agreement did not commit either country to allocation of military forces, leaving each government to determine the size and nature of its contribution.
The Canadian contribution to NORAD has always appeared minuscule when compared with that of our giant neighbour to the south, even though we have always striven to maintain our proper proportional commitment. Even if Canada supplied 10 per cent of the total interceptors available to the commander-in-chief of NORAD to meet this requirement, it would not fulfil our purely national interests. It was evident, in fact, even in 1958 when our armed forces had reached their post-war peak in
[The Deputy Chairman.]
terms of numbers, that we were unable to span the breadth of the country with interceptor aircraft. United States' interceptors were, and are, effectively carrying out what we now recognize as protection of our national sovereignty.
The original ten-year agreement, renewed in 1968 for five years and extended in 1973 for two years, was obviously aimed at defence against the manned bomber threat. However, North American air defence policy has been under constant review during past years, and mainly as a result of missile development and strategic arms limitation talks between the United States and the Soviet Union has undergone a dramatic change in priorities. Defence against the manned bomber has been de-emphasized in favour of surveillance and control of each country's sovereign airspace. I submit it is a radical change which the hon. member for Greenwood has not noticed. I hope he has, because it is a radical change in NORAD'S commitment.
Since this matter has been raised, I would also like to mention a few facts about the manned bomber threat as it exists today. While, with the growth of missile inventories, the relative importance of the manned bomber as an intercontinental threat has declined, it remains a potent weapons system. Compared to the ICBM, the bomber is more flexible and accurate and is capable of carrying a larger payload. Despite contrary opinion, the number of heavy bombers in the U.S.S.R. inventory has not significantly declined. Moreover, the capability of the Soviet fleet has been improved with the introduction of air-to-surface stand-off missiles and in-flight refuelling.
For the past several years we have been following the development of the new Soviet supersonic swing-wing bomber, nicknamed the "backfire". Several squadrons are in operational service with long-range aircraft and numbers are likely to increase with the phase-out of obsolete types. Even though the major strategic threat is from missiles, we cannot afford to let the strategic balance be upset by ignoring the bomber. We must prepare our defences against what the potential enemy is capable of doing, not against what our analysts assess his intentions to be. It should be stressed that the capability is there. They have introduced new supersonic bombers. We can only assume that these are being brought in as part of their reservoir of weapons, and not merely for show. Because we have analysed the problem as one of supersonic missiles, we still must take into account that this is in their inventory.
To take our defence apart because we analysed it as a missile threat would be leaving our gate partly open. The hon. member for Greenwood is correct that this is not the major impact of the U.S.S.R. Nor, as the old cliche goes, should we ever consider giving them a free ride. The best incentive to Soviet bomber development would be the disbandment of NORAD air defence forces. Small though they may be, and in Canada's case relatively ineffective against bombers such as the "backfire", NORAD's air defence squadrons provide a counterbalance to a known threat.
With regard to nuclear weapons, it is probably in the context of air defence that I should put the question of nuclear weapons to rest. There have been many discus-
June 5, 1975

sions in this House and elsewhere about the fact that we still have nuclear weapons on the CF-101. The minister has stated on several occasions that we have a replacement for it. It will more than likely have conventional weapons. Because of the age of the CF-101, it would be impractical at this time to spend many millions of dollars converting it from nuclear to standard weaponry. We will see the day in Canada where we will not have nuclear weapons. The day of the Bomarc is over. The day of the CF-101 will be over in five years. We will soon see a new generation of fighters which will be equipped with standard weaponry.
I also wish to discuss Canadian sovereignty and independence with regard to the NORAD agreement. While Canadians should appreciate the large American contribution to Canadian defence, our inability to "go it alone" has to some extent raised questions as to Canadian sovereignty. There is little doubt that Canada's participation in NORAD has enhanced our ability to ensure surveillance and control of Canada's airspace. On the other hand, most of the forces required to exercise sovereignty control are American, which to some extent compromises Canadian independence. However, the minister has announced that the western sector of NORAD in Canada will come under Canadian control with the establishment of new headquarters in Alberta.
One of NORAD's long-term objectives has been for us to acquire the ability unilaterally to carry out our own detection and identification functions. I welcome the minister's statement. I welcome it in the context that it will give Canada sovereignty over its own airspace in the foreseeable future. With regard to the renewal of the agreement, it is significant to note that the new agreement indicates the changing emphasis on sovereignty and air defence by according precedence to national sovereignty. In future, the primary objective of NORAD will be to assist each country to safeguard the sovereignty of its airspace, to contribute to the deterrence of attack on North America by providing capabilities for warning of attack and for defence against air attack and, should deterrence fail, to ensure an appropriate response against attack by providing for the effective use of the forces of the two countries available for air defence.
The priorities as set out here have been under study ever since publication of the white paper "Defence in the '70s". In essence, some of the proposals put forth as a result of the study suggested that the surveillance requirements of MOT and DND be integrated into a single national system and that our interceptor force be redistributed to provide an interceptor capability throughout the whole of Canada, rather than the limited areas now protected. Over a year ago DND entered into an agreement with MOT for joint acquisition and use of new, three-dimensional radars. These radars would replace current DND heavy radars, and with complementary MOT terminal radars would stretch across the country to provide surveillance and control for both military and domestic air traffic.
At the same time, and in conjunction with this requirement program, Canada and the United States are reconfiguring the present NORAD regions to emphasize the sovereignty role spelled out in the NORAD agreement.
Business of Supply
Four regional operations control centres will be established in the U.S.A. and two in Canada, one in the east at North Bay and one in the west at Edmonton. The ROCCs will replace the present NORAD regional control centres, processing all the radar detection data and controlling NORAD interceptors. The basic difference between the present regional set-up and the proposed ROCC plan is in the areas controlled. For the first time, control of Canadian airspace will rest solely with Canadians. I like that change.
As to the interceptor force, I have already addressed to some degree the inadequacies of the CF-101. We now rely on the U.S.A to provide interceptor aircraft to prosecute sovereignty violations between British Columbia and Sault Ste. Marie, but with the establishment of purely national ROCCs we will not have the same easy access to U.S resources. I might say, without being parochial, that the 409 does a fine job on the west coast of B.C.
Since the white paper recommendations were made, we have also been forced to reduce the size of our CF-101 fleet, both for reasons of economy and to enable us to stretch the life of this aircraft to 1980. However, it is no secret that our fleet of 36 operational Voodoo aircraft is now outdated and worn out. In fact, at the moment we have only a fraction of them serviceable due to engine fatigue breakdowns. These aircraft, at the best of times, can patrol only a small portion of Canadian airspace and though still possessing a capability for limited surveillance and control, will have to be replaced in the near future. I believe a lead-up time of three or four years is needed, and I sincerely hope the minister will give active consideration to the replacement of the 101 within the very near future because there is no question that the 101 has a very limited number of years of service left.
What particularly concerns me is that the breakdown of parts of the engine, caused by fatigue, has caused numerous fires in the past several years, and as a former member of Air Defence Command I consider it behooves the government to provide equipment which at least does not expose our personnel to unnecessary danger. The aircraft has served very well to this point, but we could very soon be running into serious problems associated with its age.
Looking to the future, what do we foresee for NORAD? It is likely that the integration of the civil and military radar and data assessment items will continue. The data will continue to feed into the NORAD computers as command control facilities are updated with the establishment of the ROCCs. This is simply a warning system which can be used in an emergency because of the nature of the ground installation being open to attack. It is something which the United States has studied, and perhaps in the future we shall have to look at the same thing. The extent to which Canada will be involved in this program or in the use of these facilities has not so far been determined, to the best of my knowledge.
Unfortunately, the high cost of defence is something which is extremely difficult to justify to the public in times of peace. I am speaking of peace in our own area; we all know that somewhere or other wars have been going on for a generation or so. It is very hard for the military to justify the expenditure of many millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money even for such an object as the preserva-

All these things are important, of course, but as a member of the committee on defence I am conscious of a moral tug-of-war between the need for expenditure to protect the sovereignty of Canada and the desirability of spending money in areas of social need.
Looking toward the Arctic, for instance, it is obvious we need to establish surveillance arrangements in this region, one which I regard as an increasingly important part of Canada. This is necessary if we are to claim sovereignty over the Arctic, but, as I say, we are dealing with intangible propositions and it is not always easy to convince Canadians that the heavy expenditures involved are justified. Madam Chairman, as a member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak this afternoon in this debate on the 1975-76 estimates of the Department of National Defence. In the estimates for 1975-76 there is listed under the words "Currently estimated total cost" the sum of $53,200,000 covering the cost of Canada's experimental hydrofoil, HMCS Bras D'Or. In the next column is an estimate of $230,000 which will be set aside to cover the maintenance costs of this mothballed ship during this fiscal year. When I questioned this figure before the committee as being excessive, I was informed that only $70,000 would be required for maintenance, while the balance of $160,000 is to provide for studies related to the possible application of hydrofoils in future ship construction programs.
This reply brings into question the research and development policies of the present government, especially as they apply to Canada's defence department. Obviously, if suitable studies had been made prior to the construction of the hydrofoil Bras D'Or, the $53 million spent on this experimental ship could well have been utilized in a more productive manner. It seems to me that from the very beginning we Canadians have been sold a bill of goods by the government on the value of fixed hydrofoils, and the fact that it has not been possible to date to sell this concept to any-and I emphasize "any"-of our NATO partners would indicate there is something radically wrong with this particular ship.
In light of the tremendous original cost of this project to Canada and its continuing cost even though the Bras D'Or is in mothballs, I think it is advisable to review the facts

leading up to its construction. The idea for this type of ship is, of course, not new. Half a century ago, on Cape Breton's Bras D'Or Lake, Alexander Graham Bell and F. W. Casey Baldwin were experimenting with one of their projects which they called Hydrodrome 4. When it rose from the water, supported by finlike devices attached by struts to its hull, it zoomed to 61.5 knots and established a world water speed record. Hydrodrome 4 was an early version of the present day hydrofoil, the flying ship that achieves remarkable speeds when the hull rises above the surface, reducing the friction of the vessel's contact with the water.
The present Canadian hydrofoil, Bras D'Or, named in honour of two pioneering Canadian scientists, was to be constructed for $9 million when the keel was laid at Sorel, Quebec, in 1963. However, a fire during construction added $6,500,000 to the cost and expenses skyrocketed upward from that point in time. Other setbacks occurred during construction, and the ship was finally commissioned around July, 1968. During sea trials in July, 1969, the ship reached a speed of 62 knots, which made her the fastest submarine chaser in the world. However, after a record performance near the mouth of Halifax harbour, a small crack in the foil put the ship out of commission for a year while a new centre foil was built. Following further tests, other hairline cracks developed, with serious ones occurring in the horizontal cross-member in the main hydrofoil located at the rear of the flying ship. Tenders were called for replacements costing in the vicinity of $500,000, while less serious cracks were repaired by welding.
All of these problems caused the government to decide in the fall of 1971 to put the Bras D'Or in mothballs for five years because, in the view of the then minister of national defence, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, "There appears to be no market for that type of ship". When expressing that viewpoint, the minister was obviously unaware of the opinions expressed by leading navy spokesmen concerning ships in the hydrofoil category. Commander G. L. Edwards, skipper of the Bras D'Or at that time, stated that three hydrofoils could be built for the price of one destroyer; and although the ship is designed for anti-submarine operations, he said; "You can name almost any mission for it-put missiles on it, search and rescue, fisheries protection or area surveillance. There's no way a torpedo is going to hit it when foilborne, and it goes so fast a torpedo couldn't catch it".
With all of these well founded opinions by highly placed navy personnel in favour of the hydrofoil, I cannot help but ask the question: Where did we go wrong? Obviously, officials in the defence research establishment were so keenly interested in the development of the Bras D'Or that they turned a blind eye and a deaf ear to all previous hydrofoil developments. For example, a 110-ton experimental hydrofoil, 115 feet long, with retractable foils-and I emphasize retractable foils, not fixed foils-was built by Boeing Aircraft Corporation and JM Martinac at Mar-tinac's Tacoma yard, and launched on August 17, 1962.
It was completed, named Flagstaff and placed in service on September 3, 1963, with sonar equipment installed, two guns and four 21-inch torpedo launchers, at a cost of $3,700,000. It had a forward speed of 48 knots. All of this, I point out to the committee this afternoon, was accom-
June 5, 1975

plished in the United States at a period of time before we ever started our experiment. That is why I say, Madam Chairman, that we have been misled by our government in regard to this particular project. When you compare the costs and date of completion with the track record of the builders of the Bras D'Or, you begin to understand why our NATO partners are reluctant to get involved with purchasing this type of ship in Canada.
Other models followed the Flagstaff, and the concept of a common fast patrol boat was studied by NATO officials. In September, 1970, it was decided that a retractable submerged foil craft of 140 tons, known as the PHM, as proposed by the United States navy was the vessel most suited to NATO mission requirements. In October, 1971, the U. S. indicated it would proceed at its own expense with the design of the vessel and share the results of the studies with those nations wishing to purchase PHM's. It also offered to conduct all aspects of design and development, contracting and management in co-operation with governments entering into project membership.
Since Canada is a NATO country, the results of all this research would have been freely made available to us and, what is more important, the hydrofoils developed by the United States are in constant service since the foils are retractable. The benefits are obvious, for a ship with fixed foils like the Bras D'Or draws too much water when in shallow harbours and is highly vulnerable, as the minister and his officials have found out, when it is cruising in the North Atlantic and happens to come in contact with ice pans or other obstructions.
The Boeing PHM is an all-weather, high-speed, highly-manceuvrable, missile-firing patrol craft whose development was undertaken jointly by the United States, the Federal Republic of Germany, and Italy. The construction of two lead ships was provided for by Boeing's $46.5 million design and development contract with the naval sea systems command. The American navy plans originally called for funding a total of 30 of these vessels through fiscal year 1977. Germany is planning to initiate a ten-ship procurement next summer and has awarded Boeing a contract for the phase 1 development of the German variant of the PHM. Italy has announced its intention to procure four PHM's but has not yet awarded a design contract for its distinctive version.
It should be pointed out that the Boeing PHM became an authorized NATO program project under a memorandum of understanding signed in 1972 by the three nations currently sponsoring the ship. I think that is an important fact, a point that has never been brought to the attention of this House by the government or the minister. We are still being told, "Let us wait; let us wait". While we are waiting the cost to Canadians is skyrocketing.
In view of all these facts, I believe there will be hydrofoils in our future, for we have vast areas of oceans to patrol and surveillance will have to be maintained over foreign fishing fleets. However, we cannot carry out this work with a ship like the Bras D'Or and its fixed foils. The government should face up to the fact that it has blundered badly in pursuing this type of design, and co-operate with our NATO partners in providing our navy with a hydrofoil that has been proven and operational under almost any conditions. The time and money presently
Business of Supply
being wasted can never be regained, and the opinions of our leading navy men concerning the need for operational high-speed hydrofoils should be given every consideration.
From my studies on hydrofoils, I learned that the biggest share of the hydrofoil market is military, and the biggest share of the military market is overseas. However, Boeing is moulding its hydrofoil marketing and production plans to an emerging market dominated by international military requirements, but which also involves passenger-carrying ships and those in the utility class. Admittedly, without the military programs, Boeing's commercial jet foil program could not continue, since the two programs share personnel and facilities for greater efficiency and economy.
It is difficult at this stage to predict the market for commercial hydrofoils. Some of the people in the hydrofoil industry talk of a market of a couple of hundred ships over the next ten years, but this market will have to be developed. Obviously, it is a matter of getting the boat's capabilities into areas where they are really needed and can be fully utilized. A major segment of the market will be high speed hydrofoil utility vessels to serve offshore marine operations. As this phase of offshore activity develops, non-passenger utility ships could ultimately account for as much as 90 per cent of all commercial sales.
What is Boeing doing at the present time? It is promoting the concept of regional final assembly centres around the world as a means of assuring itself a profitable production base, while meeting the worldwide sentiment for greater participation in industrial programs. The centres, which would not be owned or operated by Boeing, would purchase basic hulls from Boeing and then complete the ships for local customers.
The major prospects for these regional centres include Greece, Iran, Japan, Taiwan, Scandinavia, and the Caribbean. You will note that I did not mention Canada. It seems that everyone in every part of the world is aware of the technology that has been developed, that is, everyone except Canada and this minister who sits opposite me with his oficials.
For these reasons it seems to me that Canada is missing the boat when it comes to hydrofoil development. It is missing the boat if it continues to pin its hopes on its expensive but obsolete prototype called the Bras d'Or.
I have a couple of questions I should like to ask before I sit down, and I hope there will be a few minutes left in which the minister can answer. I should like to ask the minister why we continue to spend hundreds of thousands of tax dollars, money which I submit could urgently be used in other areas on other projects, on this Bras d'Or project? Why have we not taken advantage of the experimental work done by our NATO partner, the United States? In that way we could participate in a workable hydrofoil like the PHM, because the hydrofoil will be required for surveillance of our economic zones and for the protection of our sovereignty and our marine resources. This is a program which would in addition provide an opportunity for all our shipyards to begin production of these highly technical and versatile craft. Why have these things not been done?

Madam Chairman, I trust that all members will agree that the realization of the Canadian aims of political independence and prosperity depends on a state of international peace and security. It is assumed, therefore, that it is in Canada's direct interest that war be prevented but, if unavoidable, that it should be halted before it can escalate into a broader conflict. I also believe that hon. members will agree that large scale hostilities in any nuclear context would mean very serious results beyond our wildest imagination.
As we know, the maintenance of peace remains a United Nations' priority. It is also our belief, however, that this cannot be entrusted solely to the super powers but that other countries, including Canada, must accept and share some of the responsibility.
Canada has come to be widely respected as a country having not only the capability but, equally important, the trust and goodwill of others, which enables us to play an effective role in the maintenance of peace. No matter where our forces travel in this world the Canadian soldier is highly respected, highly trained, and a highly relied on person because of this trust. The Canadian forces military role in international peacekeeping is a vital and important aspect of the total Canadian effort.
During recent world events it has been demonstrated that this Canadian role of peacekeeping can involve a high price. However, imperfect as peacekeeping may appear to be at many times, we must realize that as long as men are

prepared to resort to force to settle disputes, Canadians must, especially in today's world, stand by to restore and maintain peace between nations.
The humanitarian role of Canada's peacekeeping forces in many areas of conflict, in alleviating suffering, and providing assistance and protection to the unfortunate innocents caught in the conflict, must also be appreciated. This Canadian role has been played very effectively in Cyprus where the United Nations force is actively involved in keeping the peace. All Canadians are deeply concerned for the safety and security of our Canadian troops and, therefore, our Canadian peacekeepers are instructed never to take chances with their lives.
Canada's experience has provided us with considerable insight into peacekeeping operations. Governments of Canada since 1946 have accepted every request the United Nations has made in this field. In addition, we have responded to requests to participate in peacekeeping type missions outside the United Nations; two in Indo China and one in Nigeria. Our 1971 white paper on defence, and the government's foreign policy review with regard to peacekeeping emphasize the continuing objective of the government to co-operate with other United Nations member countries in efforts to improve the effectiveness of peacekeeping operations, and to continue to contribute to those in which Canada can play a useful role, preferably under UN auspices.
The responsibility of carrying out these peacekeeping tasks has fallen, in the main, to our armed forces. They have served us well and have earned us an international reputation par excellence as peacekeepers. Their experience has ranged from large scale operations such as those in Korea and the Congo, down through the whole range of the peacekeeping spectrum to small United Nations observer missions. Their work has often been uncomfortable and dangerous, and some have failed to return.
I know all hon. members are proud of the troops representing Canada under the flag of the United Nations. Every member in this House today probably has constituents serving with United Nations forces in the Middle East and Cyprus, or with the UN missions in Korea, India or Pakistan. As you know, these are drawn from bases all across Canada and reflect at the same time the diversity and unity of our country. For example, a unit from my constituency, the first battalion of the Royal Canadian Regiment, 1 RCR, based in London, Ontario and commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Phil Spencer, returns tomorrow from Cyprus, having completed a six month tour. The battalion replaced the Canadian Airborne Regiment from Edmonton last December, and was replaced in turn this week by a unit from Quebec City, the second battalion of the Royal Twenty-Second Regiment.
Although the events of the past six months on Cyprus made fewer headlines than the crisis situation faced by the Canadian Airborne Regiment last summer, the tasks assumed by 1 RCR last December were no less demanding. The battalion was required to man 24 observation posts between the belligerents in Nicosia, in addition to carrying out numerous patrols in jeeps and armoured person-
June 5, 1975

nel carriers. Their area of responsibility included the capital city of Nicosia and the nearby Nicosia airport.
It was no easy task to try to maintain a ceasefire between two armed forces whose positions are in such close proximity, while coping with such hazards as poorly marked minefields. The battalion also provided humanitarian relief to many thousands of refugees made homeless by the fighting. Their efforts during the period were successful but, unfortunately, at the cost of the lives of two members of the regiment, Captain Ian Patten and Private Steven Kohlman.
The work of 1 RCR was typical of many other Canadian units on UN service. The Canadian public has come to expect that its troops will always perform in a manner which brings credit to Canada, often without thinking why this should be so. I think one of the main reasons why our troops do so well is that they are dedicated professionals, organized, trained and disciplined to carry out conventional military operations. Their high standards allow them to adapt quickly and competently to, such operations as peacekeeping activities, or giving aid to the civil authorities in areas where natural disasters have occurred, or search and rescue operations. We would do well to maintain this professionalism, not only in peacekeeping, as history has shown that our forces are often called upon to perform tasks unidentified in advance by either political or military planners. I think it important, therefore, to maintain a well trained, balanced, conventional force capable not only of meeting our current defence priorities but also any other unforeseen commitments which may arise.
In summary, peacekeeping is a difficult and often frustrating task, with results that are often not readily apparent. The value of peacekeeping has been and will continue to be questioned. It must be acknowledged, however, that both peacekeeping forces and missions have been able to calm troubled waters in situations which otherwise might have escalated into uncontrolled hostilities. We hope this has been a significant contribution to world peace.
I have always stated that Canadian soldiers, indeed Canadian veterans, policemen and firemen, are entitled to receive more money because they never know when they will run into trouble in their line of duty. We all know that this is part of their job, but I still say that they are entitled to a little extra share out of our affluence.
Furthermore, I believe that the retirement benefits of our soldiers and widows should be thoroughly updated so that they reflect the true cost of today's standard of living. At present pensions are too low, and after a soldier has served his 25 years he finds that he cannot survive on his pension and therefore is forced to seek other employment immediately. We should either allow him to stay in the service for a longer period of time or pay him a higher pension.
Canadian soldiers receive excellent training in the services, but when they are retired we have no system whereby a man could be given full credit for his training in any trade, such as by being awarded a trade certificate upon retirement. We train the man, give him expert supervision, but when we retire him we allow him to go into a no man's land, with all the knowledge he has gained in the
Business of Supply
services but with no certificate which would allow him to make a living and to compete in the private sector.
We should have agreements with provincial governments across Canada which would take into account the many years of schooling and training which soldiers have undergone so that they can receive trade licences upon retirement.
All Londoners, and in fact all Canadians, welcome back the first battalion of the Royal Canadian Regiment to their base in London, Ontario, after a well done job of six months' duration.

A new mandate in international peacekeeping and supervision undertaken by the Canadian forces in 1974 was their participation in the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force, UNDOF, in the Golan Heights area on the border between Israel and Syria. Recently this mandate has been extended in Egypt until July 24, 1975, and for UNDOF until November 30, 1975. A major increase of the contingent in Cyprus was also carried out at the request of the United Nations' Secretary General following the Turkish military intervention in July. There were no changes in other supervisory or peacekeeping operations by Canadians elsewhere during the year.
Currently Canada participates in the following operations: In the UN Truce Supervisory Organization in Palestine we have 20 officers. Their role, established in 1948, is to observe the ceasefire and to assist the parties in the application and observance of the agreements concluded between Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan, Syria and Israel. Canada has provided personnel for this operation since 1954. Also, this group provided an early United Nations presence during the October, 1973, war and assisted in the establishment of the UN Emergency Force, subsequently deployed in the Suez Canal area. Since the establishment of UNDOF in June of 1974, 90 TSO observers, including six Canadians, have been placed under the temporary operational control of UNDOF.
In the United Nations military observer group in India-Pakistan, nine Canadian forces officers were on the staff which was established in 1949 to supervise the implementation of terms of the ceasefire agreement in Kashmir between India and Pakistan. Canada also provided an air detachment of one Twin Otter aircraft, three officers and five men of other ranks.
In the United Nations Command Mixed Armistice Commission, one officer represents Canada. He is also the assistant Canadian liaison officer to the commander in chief, UN command. A sergeant assists him in his duties.
With regard to the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East, on October 6, 1973, renewed hostilities broke out between the Arabs and the Israelis. On October 22 the United Nations Security Council passed a joint USA-USSR resolution calling for a ceasefire. A similar resolution sponsored by the non-alligned countries was passed on October 25, 1973, and a ceasefire was established between Israel and Egypt.
Planning then began for the formation of a UN emergency force numbering 7,000 personnel to be deployed in

June 5, 1975

the ceasefire area. Canada and Poland were requested to provide the logistics support for the force. In early November of 1973 Canada provided a signals unit and Poland an engineer unit. Negotiations over the division of the remainder of the responsibilities continued in New York.
On November 23, 1973, it was agreed that Canada would provide a supply company, a maintenance company, a postal detachment, a military police detachment, a movement control unit, and an air transport unit consisting of two Buffalo aircraft. These elements were all in the action area by January of 1974. Poland, in addition to the engineer unit, provided a road transport company and a field hospital.
In June of 1974 the United Nations requested that Canada supply a third Buffalo aircraft to add to the two already serving with the air unit. The Canadian government agreed that additional aircraft be put into service in the Middle East, as was done in mid June. On August 9, 1974, one of the aircraft was shot down near the Syrian-Lebanese border killing nine persons on board, all members of the Canadian forces.
During July and August the headquarters of both UNEF and the Canadian contingent were moved east from Cairo to Ismailia on the Suez Canal. The majority of the Canadian forces personnel serving with UNEF are now located in this Suez location.
The present strength of the Canadian contingent which continues to provide support for the force, numbers over 900, all ranks. In the United Disengagement Observer Force until the end of May, 1974, the operations of UNEF were limited to the border area between Israel and Egypt.
Although UNDOF was established as a separate force, to date it has operated largely as an extension of UNEF. The current over-all strength of UNDOF is 1,100 with Canada providing 130 personnel from UNEF and six observers from UNTSO.
I think the armed forces are doing a wonderful job. God bless them!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, apparently the minister did not understand my question. I am referring to this letter from the Minister of Transport in 1969 which claimed that 40,000 hours of man-work would be provided to CAE in Winnipeg. This was a commitment to keep the plant going. I should like to know when these 40,000 hours of work are going to be provided to CAE because, if they are not provided in the very near future the plant is going to be closed. Can the minister tell us when he is going to live up to this? That is my question. It has nothing to do with any other firm in Winnipeg; it specifically refers to the CAE plant in Winnipeg.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have the letter that the hon. member refers to in front of me. It is the Department of Defence Production that is referred to in paragraph (c). It is not related to the responsibilities of the Department of National Defence.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, does the minister have no other knowledge of work being provided for CAE? Is he making any intervention to see that work will be provided to CAE before it folds up? Does he have any defence contracts, or knowledge of defence contracts that can be directed to CAE in Winnipeg?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am always interested in defence contracts but they are let by the Department of Supply and Services, not by the Department of National Defence.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: What about the old home town- Winnipeg?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: A lot of aerospace work, as my colleague made clear, will be going to a number of companies in Winnipeg and Manitoba. CAE is capable of bidding on this work. It has bid on some, although unsuccessfully I believe. I cannot assume responsibility for this. speechtext: Mr. Minister, it is interesting to note the promises made to CAE prior to the July 8 election. As you will remember, their business agent was your seconder at your nomination meeting. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: I want to discuss outside consultants whom the Department of National Defence hires, despite all the expertise available in the department and the department's limited working budget. I ask this of the minister: are you intervening directly in this matter? Are you considering why all this money should be pouring out to outside consultants? Do you agree that this money ought to be directed to outside consultants, and is there an actual need for their services? In other words, have you, yourself, investigated whether all these consultant studies are required? Could you give me some explanation?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, yes I have. I look at every submission which comes forward to me concerning outside consultants. I examine each one and have asked myself exactly the same questions the hon. member is asking me. I want to know if we can do the work within the Department of National Defence for which we are engaging consultants. I ask these questions, at least, on every major contract. I believe we should be able to do more "in-house" than we have in the past. In fact, we have tried to do any work for which we are competent "in-house" rather than go to outside consultants.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to direct to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) on Vote 1 of the Department of National Defence.
Mr. Chairman, I think this day is very instructive for us and it will provide information to the people of this country because they will have an opportunity to know the views of parliamentarians on the defence system of this country, the amounts invested, because the national defence estimates now amount to over $2.5 billion. It is an important department from a monetary and social standpoint.
When we talk of defence we think in terms of security and peace for all citizens of this country and if we want peace at home it must be effective elsewhere as well. If we had no potential aggressors there would be no need for us to talk of defence, armament, but such is not the case in the world. So we must accept the world as it is and stop hiding our heads in the sand to detect the enemy where he is to be found and not be afraid to point him out. That is
June 5, 1975

why tonight I will be very clear. I will deal first with NORAD and then say a few words about NATO.
After listening to the speeches made this afternoon and among others the NDP member I realized that one must really be misinformed about the intentions of the Soviet Union or be among its accomplices to talk like the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) did this afternoon, when he candidly admitted that the NORAD agreement no longer served any purpose because the U.S.S.R. is no longer threatening today. I will say, Mr. Chairman, that the U.S.S.R. is more threatening than ever in all North America. For example, we know that the quieter the U.S.S.R. is, the more it presents a velvet paw, the more it is preparing to jump on its unsuspecting victim. When we think of its conquests of Slavic countries which led to the Warsaw Pact, when we visit Germany and walk along the 35-mile long Berlin wall cutting the city in two, with only one door, and that is taking place in the 29th century, in the era of astronautics and electronic transportation systems, it is unimaginable for someone who has not seen it. Today, not daring to attack North America as it did its satellite countries for fear of the United States, it fights a psychological and tactical war faking to come to the rescue of countries surrounding North America. You have seen them in Cuba, China, Vietnam, Egypt, and you will see them again elsewhere in the hope that one day all its missiles will be pointed towards America in all directions.
I do not mean to make any prophecies, Mr. Chairman, I am just witnessing what I have under my eyes and what every member may check for himself. Hon. members who read papers have heard of the series of Russian Cosmos satellites launched by just one rocket, as announced by the TASS Agency. Those rockets circle the world in 115 minutes. I think we should be more careful than ever to protect efficiently not only Canada, by the North American continent as a whole.
I read with deep interest the statement of the Minister of National Defence to the Standing Committee on National Defence on May 1, 1975 with respect to the new territorial limits of NORAD. Part of it reads as follows:
The establishment of new territorial limits for NORAD in Canada and the United States would result in each country controlling its own air space.
Since the implementation of NORAD in 1958, the limits of air defence areas overlapped the international border; surveillance and control were exercised by both member countries.
Under the new agreement, Canada will be divided into two geographic areas of fairly equal size, each with a regional operations control centre established in Canada. A new control centre which will cost $25 million once equipped, is to be established near Edmonton, Alberta. The other one is already in operation in North Bay, Ontario.
Each of those control centres will have a staff of some 250 people. Work at the Edmonton centre will start next year, and the equipment of both centres will be chosen next year too. Computers will be used to detect, identify and control aircraft that would enter the Canadian airspace.
Since 1958, and particularly during the 60s, when I visited with the committee the general headquarters of NORAD in Colorado Springs, the crux of our whole continental defence, I had been somewhat concerned that the U.S. military authorities had supreme control over our defence system. After 17 years, the minister decided to assume greater responsibilities and to have Canada
Business of Supply
behave more as an independent country vis-a-vis its American partner.
An addition to the new control centre in Alberta, we will have near Chatham, New Brunswick, a Baker-Nunn photographic facility. This will supply information to NORAD's detection and tracking system in Colorado Springs. I believe this is a step forward in North America's air protection.
Coming now to NATO, which was created to counter the Warsaw Pact, a number of my fellow citizens wonder why we should still be keeping over 3,000 troops in Europe. Obviously, our constituents do not see the point in maintaining that European force at the same level as the domestic one, and a number of them do not understand why we should keep forces in Cyprus, in Corea and elsewhere.
I am happy that we should go on cooperating with nations requiring our participation, in the interest of peace. But I am forced to ask questions in the face of France's position. That country took its troops out of NATO. It may be argued that she is still a member in principle. But surely, if every country were to rely only on principles for its defence, we would be engulfed in principals. We are told the French government will not act as a buffer to any new attack anymore, that it will rather defend itself. These are serious enough suggestions that invite reflection.
Looking back, I would not condemn the French authorities. They did more than their part during World War II. And I wonder whether the delay by allied countries to help France is not one reason for the withdrawal. Therefore, it may be because of delays in NATO decisions that France is losing some of its confidence. In fact, in some araes, even if we maintain our forces, a great part of the arms or military equipment used belongs in another age.
At certain times, especially when I went there for a visit, I wondered if our men were not there to serve a museum caretakers. Fortunately, the minister in his statement has brought new hope of modernization, without which our army would be nothing but Canadian folklore in Europe. The minister said that the defence budget has increased, but I would like him to note that the major part of the increase if due mostly to salary increase. The minister also talks about the quality of our men; we never doubted their quality. But it is useless to proclaim that one Canadian soldiers is worth five Russian soldiers; the most important thing is that he should be as well equipped as the Russians.
It is about the same situation as in hockey; we are constantly repeating that we have the best athletes in the world, but this does not prevent us from taking humiliating beatings at the hands of the Russians. We should profit from this lesson at least in the military area.
I would also like to call the attention of the minister on useless spendings, when the money is not simply thrown away, as my colleague from Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) mentioned. I know that this is a delicate subject for the minister and that it is his major source of concern. But this should not stop him from being even more careful. Our military forces, whether at sea, on land or in the air, which have the duty to protect Canadian sovereignty, to

June 5, 1975
Business of Supply
help civilian authorities to ensure the control and the security of our national territory, to cooperate with the American forces in the joint defence of North America, in maintaining peace in Europe and elsewhere, have no right to disappoint Canadian taxpayers by taking part in schemes which are unworthy of their mission.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are the few comments I wanted to make tonight.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during this debate on the Department of National Defence estimates the question of the requirement to safeguard Canada's sovereign interests must be kept in the forefront of our deliberations. Of great interest in this respect is the government's current review of the need for a new long range patrol aircraft. I would like to comment briefly on this subject which will have such a major impact on DND expenditures.
The potential for challenges to Canada's sovereignty and security take both non-military and military forms and arise principally from Canada's vast size and relatively small population, her abundance of natural resources, the length of her shores, the size of the water areas which are of direct concern to her and the fact that historically we have identified and allied ourselves politically and militarily with those nations which share our perceptions of individual freedom and justice and our way of life.
One important component of the military and civilian resources devoted to monitoring and defending against both military and non-military threats has been the Argus aircraft of Maritime Command of the Canadian forces.
The Argus was introduced into service in 1958 and was a good maritime patrol aircraft in its day; its equipment was among the best available at that time, and its range made it possible to conduct long patrols over the far reaches of the Atlantic and North Pacific Oceans. Over the years, more modern and effective surveillance equipment has been developed and the Argus is now limited in capability compared with other aircraft in this role. The capability of its surveillance devices is relatively limited, the aircraft is slow, and the long flight times required for patrols results in high crew fatigue because of noise and vibration. The aircraft engines, and installed equipment are getting old and are expensive to maintain. The standard fuel used by the aircraft is now available at only four locations in Canada.
Therefore, on the basis of the policy outlined in the government white paper "Defence in the Seventies", extensive studies of maritime force capabilities conducted within the Department of National Defence, and the fact that continued operation of the Argus was not cost effective, the Minister of National Defence obtained cabinet approval in May, 1972, to examine in detail the possibility of obtaining suitable replacement aircraft. An interdepartmental office was established in September, 1972, and initial studies were concluded with five aircraft companies, including Canadair.
Upon receipt and evaluation of the proposals received, it was recommended that studies be continued with the two most suitable contractors, Boeing and Lockheed, and cabi-

net agreed. The studies are in their final stage at this time and it is expected that a submission to cabinet will be made in the near future. It is now timely to review the challenges facing Canada which the government must weigh in arriving at its final decision on the LRPA proposal.
With respect to non-military challenges to Canadian sovereignty, of paramount interest is the enforcement of Canadian laws and the ability of Canada to maintain its sovereignty and jurisdiction over land and sea areas of Canadian interest. The challenge, therefore, lies in any attempt to infringe upon these laws, particularly as such infringements would affect the resources of the sea and the seabed, and as they would affect the marine environment in waters of Canadian interest, including the Arctic, coastal and continental shelf areas.
While other government departments are charged with the task of policing violations of Canadian law in Canadian waters of interest, DND has the ultimate responsibility to ensure that Canadian sovereignty and jurisdiction are maintained. With respect to these challenges, therefore, it is necessary for DND to conduct surveillance of these areas, to assist other departments in their surveillance tasks, and to provide a control capability to back up other departments in their enforcement of Canadian laws.
The potential for external, non-military challenges to Canada's maritime and Arctic sovereignty and jurisdiction is very real and recent developments have heightened awareness of this potential. The U.S. decision to proceed with construction of a pipe line across Alaska and to ship North Slope oil from Alaska to U.S. West Coast ports in supertankers has increased the prospect of major oil spills off the coast of British Columbia. Current and prospective shortages of energy and other basic world commodities have heightened national and international interest in the resource potential of the Canadian Arctic and the continental margin.
The basic concern, nevertheless, remains that of the possibility of foreign infringements of Canadian laws establishing the extent and governing the use of Canada's territorial sea, internal waters, enclosed fishing zones, pollution control zones, and regulating exploration for and exploitation of the resources of the seabed subject to Canadian jurisdiction, and of Canada's Arctic territories.
Infringements of this kind are most likely to occur in areas where Canada's right to exercise jurisdiction is not fully accepted internationally and, at least at the outset, would probably be non-military in character. They would, therefore, be of primary concern to those civil departments and agencies of the federal government to which, under Canadian law, responsibility for regulation and enforcement has been assigned. The possibility, however, cannot be excluded that a determined challenge could be supported by the display or limited use of military force, as occurred in the recent fisheries dispute between Britain and Iceland.
These concerns are growing, as evidenced during the recent Law of the Sea Conference, as a consequence of the concept of an exclusive economic zone or patrimonial sea extending not less that 200 miles off a state's coast. Within this zone the state would exercise the sole responsibility for resource management, and enjoy either exclusive or
June 5, 1975

preferential rights in the exploitation of both living and inanimate resources. The implications for Canada of such a broadening of its rights and responsibilities as a coastal state are important. Law is seldom self-enforcing; it is for consideration whether the greater range of interests and greater geographical extent of the areas subject to Canadian jurisdiction would lead to a larger requirement than at present for surveillance capabilities to detect infringements of Canada's legal rights, and also for control capabilities to ensure that those rights were respected.
An area which must be considered as a special case when discussing challenges to Canadian sovereignty is the Arctic. At first glance there appears to be little possibility of direct threats in Canada's Arctic; far more concern is expressed over the possible unauthorized exploitation of the resources of this area, and of the possibility of pollution which is far more damaging in its ecological effects in the Arctic than it would be elsewhere. The non-military challenge in the Arctic includes such things as the unauthorized drilling of oil wells and the unauthorized use of Canadian waters by foreign vessels.
Although a number of federal agencies are on the ground throughout Canada's Arctic, a military force, showing its presence in that area on a regular basis, does much to re-affirm Canada's sovereignty. Further precise definition of the various challenges in Canada's Arctic will evolve in time, but it is evident that a possibility exists for a variety of challenges in this area, and a capability is required to meet these challenges as they arise.
Turning to the essentially military challenges to Canadian sovereignty, the government has outlined four objectives for the Department of National Defence. In order of priority, these are the defence of Canada, the defence of North America, contributions to the NATO alliance, and contributions to international peacekeeping operations.
During discussions on the requirement for an LRPA, much has been said of the ability of this aircraft to support national development by doing tasks for other government departments. However, Canada's armed forces provide, to the extent possible in this interdependent world, the means by which Canada can assert its sovereignty through an ability to defend itself. In addition, through representation on international military councils and contributions to international military forces, the armed forces also contribute to the defence of a wider area, and make it possible for Canada to influence the decisions, military, political and economic, of her allies. It is also true, in a military context, that providing for the defence of North America and contributing to the NATO alliance are the most effective ways of ensuring we can fulfill the first priority task, the defence of Canada.
The balance of forces between the U.S.S.R. and the United States is predicted to act as a stable deterrent to major war because both nations possess the capability to inflict upon the other an unacceptable level of destruction in retaliation for a first strike attack. Various agreements have been made, and negotiations are now being conducted which are designed to preserve this balance of power
Business of Supply
and to ensure that neither nation believes it necessary to enter into further expensive arms build-ups.
A Canadian long range maritime patrol aircraft would contribute to the stability of this situation, because for a deterrent to be credible its military components must be effective. An LRPA would also give Canada the capability to maintain its national security posture by enabling her to detect potentially hostile subsurface activity of any kind in the water approaches to her shores, including the very large continental shelf area.
Canada must continue to review its requirement for maritime forces to act as a deterrent against threats to its security and challenges to maritime jurisdiction and sovereignty. The fundamental need is for maritime surface and air forces possessing a range of capabilities and the degree of flexibility in employment which will permit them to respond promptly to sudden changes in the intensity or magnitude of particular threats or challenges. Because of its speed, range, and equipment capabilities it would appear that an LRPA would form a most important part of the air element of this force. Its speed would permit it to respond quickly to detected or suspected challenges, its range would permit it to reach any part of the vast areas which are of national interest, and its equipment would permit it to detect and, if the government decided, to control activities which are not acceptable to the government.
It is also clear that such an aircraft would have an inherent capability to contribute effectively to the support activities of other departments by the addition of a few specialized sensors for a wide range of activities, such as ice reconnaissance, wildlife determinations, and special agricultural problems. Thus there is great flexibility in such an aircraft.
Finally, I wish to say a word about industrial benefits. It is apparent that if the government is to spend the large sums of money required for a new long range patrol aircraft, such a purchase must be arranged so as to maximize the benefit to Canadian industry,-in particular the Canadian aerospace industry for which the government continues to express concern. We on this side of the House will continue to give full support to the ministers during their deliberations on this very expensive program, because it will have such an impact on Canada's long term capabilities to ensure that we do retain the control of our resources, our sovereignty, and our way of life.
Canada has been blessed with many very capable leaders within the ranks of our armed forces. I would be remiss in this debate if, as an example, I did not mention people such as General Donald Holmes, his officers, and men and women of all ranks who are giving Canada an outstanding image throughout the Middle East. They are held in the highest esteem by all parties in the present dispute in that area. They are respected and looked up to by all other United Nations contingents present in the Middle East. Their expertise, discipline, and fairness tempered with firmness, have won for them the respect of all.
General Holmes is a soldier, a statesman, a diplomat, a politician in a sense, and a gentleman all wrapped up in one man. As commanding officer of our United Nations contingent in the Middle East, he is setting the pace for his personnel. He is setting an example for everyone, and

June 5, 1975
Business of Supply
above all he and our military personnel have done more than any other government department could possibly do to promote the image of Canada abroad and to give Canada a tremendously favourable rapport with all national groups. It is my hope that when General Holmes returns next fall we will be able to invite him into the Speaker's gallery and have parliament give him the recognition he deserves.
Many people have told me, both Israelis and Egyptians as well as members of other United Nations contingents, that without our 1,037 military personnel in the Middle East the United Nations would not be able to operate nearly as effectively as it does. There are 37 women in that number. Dedication is also the name of the business of our armed forces. One has only to think of men like General Clay Beattie in Cyprus who, with the loyalty and integrity of all those who have served under him, has given so much of his life to bring about peace on that troubled island.
No matter where our armed forces go in the world they retain their excellent discipline, perform their jobs effectively, put their expertise to work, exercise common sense, and keep cool heads. This can be largely attributed to the fact that we have a volunteer force, that our personnel are in the armed forces because they want to be there and because they are interested in what they are doing. In Europe our NATO forces are respected by all NATO partners and are well received by the local people. Military attaches in capitals around the world form another group who uphold Canada and build a constructive image. This parliament owes the members of our armed forces our sincere plaudits and a wealth of national gratitude.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I might ask the parliamentary secretary one question. I listened to his treatise with great care. Does he really think, in view of the background that commenced in 1968 when the Prime Minister first became Prime Minister of this country and said he had decided to withdraw from NATO-in fact, at one time we thought there was going to be a complete withdrawal in view of the way the armed forces have been downgraded-that we have any chance of defending ourselves by air, land or water?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I may answer the hon. gentleman's question, we do not intend to downgrade the forces. We have exceptional expertise in our armed forces in this country. Contrary to the unbalanced thinking that some people have been expressing, new equipment has been ordered for our armed forces to help them do the job, and more is on order. I have just discussed one of these major programs. I am not a pessimist when it comes to the Canadian armed forces. I am a strong supporter of them, as are many people on the benches of this party over here. I know I am speaking for many members on these benches when I say they have our full support.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words about a matter which is not easily computed in terms of dollars and cents, or specifically included in any vote or even allowed for in the estimates. I want to talk for a few minutes about the reduction in the morale of our armed forces, and to ask a few questions about how it can

be restored to the high level which used to be an integral characteristic of the military.
We have heard discussions as to whether the major roles of our armed forces are as valid today as when they were first enunciated and, indeed, whether the troops we have, greatly reduced in strength, are adequate to the tasking. These are not new questions. I have heard them raised many times by members of the armed forces, certainly during the time I was a member of the National Defence College, and subsequently. Obvious to me on a recent visit to our bases in Lahr and Baden-Solingen were the unease and anxiety felt by many in the forces as Canada's role in NATO undergoes another of its perennial reviews-anxiety and unease about the maintenance of our NATO contingent and its possible reconfiguration.
I want to suggest that lack of information and inadequate communications significantly undermine morale, but much can be done to correct this problem without increasing expenditures from the public purse.
People in the military, and in military communities, are anxious and uneasy mainly because they do not know what is going on, where they are headed, and if things will improve, change radically, or further deteriorate in the months ahead. What is being looked for is not information of a highly classified nature vital to the security of the country, but day to day routine explanations that would make day to day living much easier.
I just want to mention a few of these agents that attack morale in armed forces communities. When departmental expenditures are reduced, or when there is no growth in real dollar terms as at the present time, the first area to be short changed is the maintenance of living quarters.
Time and again I have heard and seen legitimate complaints about living standards in PMQs' homes which, because of their shortcomings, cannot help but depress the occupants. These are not very happy homes for wives and children when they are much below the standard of other living accommodations in the general area. I know this to be particularly true at the Kingston base. Painting and refurbishing of homes, the fixing of appliances, and general improvements to property may seem like small items when compared with the acquisition of new LRPA or tanks, but from the over-all point of morale they are vitally important.
I would suggest that the minister should be in a position to let people know, certainly well in advance of steep rent increases, when they can expect some improvement in their living quarters. What about future plans for PMQs?
An armed forces base and the inter-relationship it has with its neighbouring community or communities have a very direct bearing on morale. Let me cite an example. A few months ago in an effort to economize on what was obviously considered peripheral and superfluous by the minister and his staff, the order was given to reduce the number of regular armed forces bands from nine to five. This was done with little or no thought to the incalculable value that accrues to the armed forces because of the high esteem in which these bands are held by men, women and children throughout neighbouring communities. Fortunately, after sufficient pressure was brought to bear, and sufficient reasoned argument was put forward, the minis-
June 5, 1975

ter saw the light and reversed the decision, enabling the bands to remain to contribute to the military and cultural life of Canada. Once again the intervening months of uncertainty, procrastination, and lack of communication added to morale problems among the forces.
The military educational establishments are another example where the future is uncertain and cloudy. It is estimated that it costs five times as much to send a student through Royal Military College as through Queen's University. Anyone who has had any exposure to RMC will know it is a fine institution with proud history and tradition. Nevertheless, one must wonder if it will continue to be operational at a cost five times that of public universities.
The people in these military institutions, staff, students and civilians, are all understandably uneasy. Perhaps there are those in the inner circle who know the long-range plans for these educational institutions, but how much better it would be to communicate that knowledge to the community at large, thus avoiding speculation and rumour which can so easily lead to distortion of the real objectives. It would not take much in the way of public expenditure to supply that information, but it would net incalculable benefits in public understanding and support, and in strengthening of morale. So I would ask, what about the future for military educational institutions?
Primarily because of the reduction in the strength of our armed forces over the years our military hospitals are not being fully utilized. For the most part these are well equipped facilities capable of handling much more traffic than they presently bear. Because of under-utilization the future of some of these hospitals is in doubt.
I am not unaware of the difficulties that arise in working out federal-provincial fiscal relations to make these hospitals available for the needs of dependents of members of the armed forces, but through you, sir, I would urge the minister to press ahead with this kind of arrangement. In any event, I would urge that he make the civic officials in neighbouring communities aware of all the facts so that adequate advanced planning can be carried out jointly with DND to make the most effective use of these hospitals in the future. Open lines of communication would dispel a lot of the doubt and uncertainty that surround the future of these hospitals. So, I would ask, what about the future of our military hospitals?
Better communications, better programming, and better reporting to our armed forces abroad on what is taking place in Canada would do a great deal to boost the morale of people in the service. I know we have CBC outlets in Lahr and Baden-Solingen and elsewhere, but I am surprised that the amount of programming from Canada is so limited. Better mail service, if such a thing were possible, and distribution of Canadian newspapers and magazines would work wonders. It all seems so obvious that it should not need saying. The same is true for the students in our schools on bases abroad. They are interested in what is taking place currently in Canada. They are thirsty for information and keen to get up-to-date material, something which they so consistently lack. So I would ask the minister about better communications to our armed forces personnel overseas.
Business of Supply
These things, I have mentioned do not require elaborate redirection of huge sums in these estimates, but homes, hospitals, educational institutions, and communications are just as important to the members of our armed forces and their dependants as they are to other Canadians. I hope that when the minister speaks he will have something to say on how the maintenance and operations of these facilities can be improved because the outcome has such a bearing on the improvement of morale.

Mr. Chairman, there are just two subjects on which I should like to make a few comments. If I gave the minister a dozen guesses, I am sure he would guess correctly on the first two.
As I am sure he realizes, I listened with interest to the conversation between the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the Minister of National Defence with respect to certain promises that were made in Winnipeg during May and June of 1974.
I think what I enjoyed most tonight was hearing the minister make so many references to the Department of Supply and Services. I have a fairly good memory of what goes on in election campaigns, but I do not remember the Department of Supply and Services being mentioned in Winnipeg last summer. It was the Minister of National Defence, with the assistance of course of the right hon. Prime Minister, who was going to protect and restore the aerospace industry in Manitoba. As the minister realizes, he is not only the only minister in the cabinet from Manitoba but he is also the Minister of National Defence, and he is in a position to try to do something about those promises that were made last summer.
I should like to emphasize in particular that in those tragic days when we were losing the Air Canada overhaul base from Winnipeg, we were assured that there would be certain replacements. One of the replacements was the work to be given to CAE Industries. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is quite right in protesting about the way in which CAE Industries are being allowed to phase out of the picture, for it looks as though that is what will happen because of the direction in which the government is moving.
I ask, therefore, that the Minister of National Defence recover some of that enthusiasm for strengthening the position of the aerospace workers in Winnipeg that was so evident in May and June of 1974.

speechtext: We need another election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58

The Leader of the Opposition has a suggestion which I think many people in this country would welcome. Many are wondering whether the vote went the right way last July 8.
When I speak of the minister's enthusiasm for the promises that he and the Prime Minister made, I am doing this not just from what I read in the papers, saw on television, and heard on the radio, but it is also based on the fact that he and I were on the same program one night in a television studio and I sensed close at hand that he really believed that if he got re-elected, and the Liberals with

June 5, 1975
Business of Supply
him, the aero industry in Winnipeg would be in a much better position.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: It is.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
The minister says that these things are being achieved. The trouble is that it is a long, slow process, and I am afraid that we will not really get the enthusiasm back until the next election, and then of course it will depend on who nominates the Minister of National Defence in Winnipeg South.
The other item about which I wish to have another word with the minister-and he knows it very well-is the question of the pensions of retired members of the armed forces.
I was pleased to hear the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works say this afternoon that this is an area in which we should do a lot better for the members of the armed forces. I was pleased to hear the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence say more or less the same thing in the speech that he made this evening. I suspect that in the armed forces in pension matters probably the most prevalent grievance is the fact that when members of the armed forces go on retirement and draw their pensions, if they are not yet 60 years of age there is no annual cost of living supplement for them as there are for public servants and for many other persons in receipt of pensions.
This is a subject that I have raised repeatedly. I also raise it with respect to retired members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I receive from the ministers responsible for both of these departments the assertion that these things have to be kept in line with other pension plans, and therefore they have to discuss the whole matter with the President of the Treasury Board. I also get the assurance every time from the Minister of National Defence or from his parliamentary secretary when he answers my questions on "late shows" that the matter is still being studied.
Perhaps this was not as serious an issue some years ago when inflation was not quite so rampant, and I understand the argument, about retired members of the armed forces being in an age bracket when perchance they can get other employment if it is available to them, but in these times of rapid inflation when most of the pensions which come under the aegis of the government are escalated in accordance with the rise in the cost of living-it is significant that in most cases they lag behind it-there is nothing for the retired armed forces individuals who are not yet 60 years of age. The minister writes letters to these people, and then we get copies of the letters, in which he points out that when such an individual reaches the age of 60, he may have five or ten years of percentage points to collect and by that time he may, in the year in which he is 60, pick up an escalation of 30 per cent or 40 per cent. But it is "the meantime" that bothers the retired armed forces individual when inflation is rising so rapidly.
I wonder tonight if the minister can say anything that is more hopeful about this matter than he has said on previous occasions when all he has told me the matter is still under study.
