speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a very brief comment to make, and it relates specifically to a question to the Minister of National Defence. I refer to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence hearing of last May 6 when the minister was a witness, and I raised certain matters relating to the Suffield Defence Research station. I am sure the minister is well aware of this matter. I asked him if he would give me a written reply to a rather detailed letter I wrote to him last October 31. To date I have not received an answer, and I thought it was significant that at the following committee meeting the acting deputy minister led off in his opening statement and made reference to my request for that answer, which has still not been received. I just want to focus attention on this matter by reading one short paragraph out of that letter, and I think this will bring to light my special concern. It reads as follows:
I would like to now ask you to very seriously consider the possibility of allowing the Suffield Research Establishment to continue in its traditional and "new look" type of operations indefinitely. Such an announcement would do much to restore confidence, morale and esprit de corps to a very dedicated and able staff, who sincerely want to continue doing a top job at Suffield and remain in the Medicine Hat-Redcliff community and eventually retire there.
That is just one paragraph, and I would appreciate it if the minister would respond.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
The hon. member for Medicine Hat and I have discussed this matter many times, both privately and in committee, and I can assure him that the detailed and very thoughtful letter he has addressed to the department is under consideration. My reply is being prepared in the department, and he will receive answers to the questions raised in his letter very shortly.
As I was saying a few moments ago when I thought I could have the floor, I welcome the opportunity to respond to the statements which have been made on both sides of the House today and to answer some of the questions to which I have not been able to reply while hon. members were addressing them to me.
First, I would like to say that I particularly welcome the very keen interest in national defence which has been evidenced on both sides of the House. It was clear to me this afternoon, and again this evening, that whatever
Business of Supply
deficiencies there may be in our equipment or in the amount of money available to the Department of National Defence, there is one matter on which all hon. members seem to be agreed, and that is the quality of service and the dedication to Canada provided by the men and women of the Canadian armed forces.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
I was particularly pleased to hear the hon. member for London East, who is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works, when he said earlier today that members of the Canadian armed forces on peacekeeping duties are men who can be trusted:- those were his words-by all. This thought, and the high degree of professionalism which the Canadian armed forces possess, is something which has been evident to me and which I have seen whenever I have visited the Canadian forces on peacekeeping duties, on their NATO responsibilities in Germany, on basis or across Canada. I am pleased that this was reflected in the debate today.
In opening the debate the hon. member for Victoria referred to the obsolete equipment of the Canadian forces. This is a subject to which there is reference quite often, both in the media and by members of the House, and I think there is a good deal of misinformation about the standard of our equipment. For that reason I would like to name just a few items on the approved capital program. Out of a list which I have here of some 33 major capital programs, I will mention only the following to indicate the very considerable extent of our new equipment purchases.
In the sea element we have approved the Sea King helicopter, improvement and modernization, for some $41,600,000. We have purchased a diving tender for some $6,600,000.
In the land element there are a number of major purchases. I think those hon. members interested in the land forces will want to know the extent of the modernization of our equipment. The program includes some 2,848 1 !4 ton trucks for a total cost of $69,960,000; 489 5-ton trucks for $27,353,000; heavy anti-armoured weapons, the TOW missile for $30,097,000; the Blowpipe air defence system $38 million; very high frequency radio $9 million, and high frequency radios $6 million.
I am not going to read the whole list, Mr. Chairman, but for those such as the hon. member for Victoria who say our equipment is obsolete I ask them to look at these figures. They will then realize that although some of our equipment is getting old we have a lot of new equipment which members of our armed forces are using in an increasingly effective way.
In the air element we have added five Hercules aircraft, the C-130, at a cost of $30 million, and eight Chinook medium helicopters for $42 million. Replacement of LORAN navigation system for selected aircraft is $6,800,000. In a more general category the Samson system, the strategic communications system, will cost $45 million. This is what is going on week by week and month by month in National Defence to improve the standard of our equipment.

June 5, 1975
Business of Supply
As I said in committee the other day, I am disappointed that hon. members keep talking about obsolete equipment. Certainly there is some, but from now on we should keep a more balanced outlook. If we talk about the old, let us also talk about the new.
I should also like to point out that we are continuously endeavouring to increase the proportion of the budget going to capital expenditures. The proportion for new equipment and construction in 1974-75 was 10.55 per cent, and in 1975-76 we estimate it will be 12.3 per cent, or some $346 million.
In relative terms, although our over-all defence expenditures are slated to increase by 11.6 per cent, the capital expenditures will be boosted by some 31 per cent over last year. I would ask hon. members to think about that figure when talking about capital expenditures. It is up 31 per cent over last year. I particularly want to point out that a large portion of the capital expenditures, about 72 per cent, will go to the purchase of new equipment.
We have approved major capital equipment programs amounting to some $530 million over the next few years, and over 43 per cent of this will be to re-equip the land forces; sea will receive 16 per cent; air 29 per cent, and capital equipment programs common to all will amount to 12 per cent.
The hon. member for Victoria made reference to the Callaghan report. I should like to point out that where allied military trade and co-operation are concerned, the Callaghan report recommends using the United States-Canada defence production sharing program as a model.
We should all be proud of the fact that Canada has been a leader when it comes to NATO industrial co-operation and standardization. For example, we are acquiring the TOW anti-tank missile from the United States and the Blowpipe anti-aircraft missile from the United Kingdom. Both these purchases were made against offsetting sales of Canadian equipment to our NATO allies.
Our allies are increasingly using Canadian manufactured equipment, mainly in the field of electronics, such as aircraft simulators, sonars and sonobuoys, crash position indicators, and computing equipment, a significant proportion of which was developed by and for the Department of National Defence.
I should like to make a brief reference to the comment of the hon. member for Greenwood. He asked me for a definition of surveillance. I would say in brief reply that airspace surveillance is the means of determining what is going on in Canadian air space. It is accomplished primarily through the use of radars. Positive identification in abnormal circumstances can only be achieved by visual observation by a pilot in a high performance aircraft.
I should also like to say to the hon. member for Greenwood, who expressed concern about the number of our interceptors, that we are now using 44 101 Voodoos, a reduction of 12 from the 56 that were in use last year.
I should like to thank the hon. member for Abitibi for his very obvious understanding of the needs of national defence and his recognition of the importance of the armed forces to Canada.

I want to turn to the remarks made by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. I have had only a few moments to obtain information and to think about the questions, which are of very great importance to the armed forces. I would agree with her that the subject of morale is perhaps one of the most important matters that all of us who are concerned with the armed forces should be thinking about. In the widest sense I believe that morale is achieved by having a sense of purpose, a sense of the importance of the work that has to be done. Personally I hope to be able to convey to the armed forces, if they do not already realize it, that their work is doubly important-not only in their duty of protecting Canada but also as I have said many times, their work in a number of other ways-in improving Canada and bringing out all of the hidden benefits of their training and education, and their development of the north, assistance to youth, and so on.
Looking at the rather narrower but still important areas mentioned by the hon. member, I think she has raised very valid questions. The first is housing our PMQs. I am able to say that we have a program for improving and renovating PMQs which will amount to some $4,758,000.
It would take me too long to go into each item in detail, but military colleges were also mentioned. I have been aware of the fact that the cost per student is much higher at RMC, College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean or Royal Roads than at Queen's University or other universities. I think the answer partly is that universities do not provide military and academic training, but that military colleges provide everything which universities provide and a lot more, including board and living accommodation. It is really not possible to compare what it costs to train a cadet at RMC, a cadet who is provided with meals, housing, and athletic and military training, with what it costs to educate a student at Queen's, a student who attends lectures from 9 to 5, or 10 to 3, or whatever the time may be, but who pays for everything else outside. We must consider these differences.
In addition, we must look at the quality of instruction at military colleges and realize that the quality of training, and the training in leadership, cannot be measured in terms of dollars per student. Therefore, to answer the question, I think that military colleges have an important place and a good future, as we have confirmed by our dollar commitment. We will be spending on the three military colleges some $17,376,000.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands mentioned hospitals. I realize they are underutilized and we must examine their best uses in Kingston and other locations. I can only say that our belief in the usefulness of the hospitals is demonstrated by our commitment to spend some $9,445,000 on improving military hospitals.
I think the hon. member's last question concerned communications. I am proud of how Air Transport Command provides mail, parcels and communications of all kinds to our personnel in NATO and on peacekeeping duty. That is the report I usually receive, although there may be isolated instances of complaint. As I have said before, I think the mail service we provide is perhaps better than that provided to civilians in the rest of Canada.
June 5, 1975

I am afraid I will not have time to answer all hon. members who have spoken. Earlier today the hon. member for Annapolis Valley said that it is necessary to build a momentum of public opinion behind national defence and in support of national defence. I agree with him on that point. In a democracy such as ours, public opinion in the long run determines the size of our defence budget. As an example I should like the Canadian public to be far more aware than it is of the growth of the number of weapons and armaments in the Warsaw Pact countries. A number of hon. members touched on this point today. I want the Canadian public to be as aware as we are of that growth in military capability, which is well beyond that needed for defence needs. Only if the public becomes aware of this can we generate the kind of public support needed for a larger defence budget. I agree with what was said in this respect.
The suggestion of the hon. member for Annapolis Valley that we have not made our defence options known is not correct. We have made a number of defence options clearly known. They have been reported in the press. I have talked about the options in Europe and said that we would either maintain land forces and an air capability, or an all-air, or an all-land capability. We are studying those options in the structure review which is now before the cabinet. We have not been reluctant to discuss our options.
I see that my time has nearly run out. I think it would be appropriate for me to conclude with the statement made earlier this year by the Chief of the Defence Staff, General Dextraze. It is a statement with which I wholeheartedly agree, and which I believe describes the Canadian armed forces.
General Dextraze said:
The Canadian forces continue to meet their assigned commitments in a highly professional manner. The operational readiness of the Canadian forces continues to be maintained at a high level; morale is good; we have effectively met all the challenges presented to us. Our forces, whether serving in Canada, with NATO in Europe, or with the United Nations around the globe continue to contribute to the maintenance of world peace and stability.
To conclude in my own words, I want the Canadian armed forces not only to respect their heritage, which I know they do, but also to be convinced in their own minds that the tasks which they perform today and the responsibilities that they accept today are of vital importance to Canada and to all Canadians. I should like all Canadians to be convinced, as I am, that the armed forces are important and, in fact, essential not only to the protection but also to the improvement of our Canadian way of life.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to express my appreciation to those members who participated in today's debate, which was long overdue. It is good that we came out of our secret committee rooms, and said in public what we think about defence. Perhaps we can create some interest on the part of the population or on the part of members.
First, I should like to reply to the Minister of National Defence, who criticized me for saying that we use obsolete equipment. I can tell him why I said our equipment is obsolete. Take the Centurion tank, which was first produced in 1946, but is still our main battle tank in Europe. When I was thinking of obsolete equipment I was thinking
Business of Supply
of the Bofors gun which forms our perimeter defence at our airfield at Lahr. The Bofors was not a good gun in 1942.
I was also thinking of the Voodoo aircraft which, according to another hon. member who spoke, has been grounded. The Voodoo, or CF-101, is our first line of defence at home. It is not in use with the United States regular forces, but is used by the national guard. They are going to drop the aircraft next year, because it is obsolete. The minister told us in committee that it would go out of Canadian use some time in the early 1980s, at least five years after the United States National Guard considered it too obsolete to be used. That is why I used the word obsolete when talking about our equipment.
Also, I was thinking of the Argus aircraft, which has been flying faithfully and well, but for far too many years. Right now, in the estimates we are considering, not one dime has been set aside for the new LRPA. The long-range patrol aircraft is a long way off.
I was also thinking of our naval forces when I talked about obsolete equipment. Although our navy has four very sophisticated new DDH 280s, it has no other ships under construction. As the lead time for new ship construction is between five and six years, I assume that within five or six years we may, if we start now, equip our naval forces with new equipment. That is why I said that our present equipment is obsolete.
The minister boasts that we are increasing our equipment from 10 per cent to 13 per cent, which he translates arithmetically to be an increase of 30 per cent. That is correct. The equipment budget is up from 10 per cent to 13 per cent, as he said.
Let me read one paragraph from the Thomas A. Callaghan report to which the minister referred. It says:
The percentage of the British defence budget spent on equipment has fallen from 42 per cent in 1965-66 to 37 per cent in 1973-74. The German defence budget shows a steady decline in the investment ratio, from a peak of 46.2 per cent in 1967 to a low of 29.0 per cent in 1972, with only slight improvement to 29.3 per cent in 1973. The American investment ratio has fallen almost 20 percentage points, to 29.8 per cent in the 20 years from FY '54 to FY '74-
This is the reason our equipment is obsolete. We are in the 8, 9, 10, 11 per cent bracket. In order to keep a modern force, the others are in the 30 to 40 per cent bracket. Moving from 10 per cent to 13 per cent is nothing to boast about.
Today we covered in general terms a lot of the problems of defence. We did not go into great detail because we have done that in committee. I would like the general public to know that we have asked questions in committee. We have had eight committee meetings on these estimates. They were noted for our inability to get the information we requested from the department.
We do not yet know where the Falcon aircraft are; or the terms of reference for our senior officials at NORAD. We do not know if we are going to sign a contract for LRPA or not. We do not know what the minister or Prime Minister means, but they say we will keep up our commitment. The commitment will be what they think it will be. They

June 5, 1975
Fort Garry
reserve the right to translate that word, and will give their meaning of it at some later date.
When we ask point blank if our manpower and soldiers in Germany are going to be reduced, we cannot get an answer yes or no. We get the weasely answer that we will keep up our commitment to suit our allies.
I see my time is almost up. I want to thank again those who participated. I want at this time to thank the distinguished chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, the hon. member for Labelle, who has done a great job. He capped it today by contributing positive suggestions. I personally thank him, and those members on my side who did so much work preparing for and participating in the debate today.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hear someone across the way saying this is new members' night. In accordance with the agreement that was reached this afternoon, I wish to raise a grievance. The understanding is that I shall take not more than half the time between now and ten o'clock, leaving the other half for a response by a representative of the government.
There are times when I wish it were possible to put on Hansard something other than words, some appropriate picture or, perhaps even better, an appropriate cartoon. There is no question but that the Printing Bureau could do this, but of course it would take unanimous consent or an amendment to the British North America Act to make it possible.
At least I can describe the cartoon which I have in my hand. It appeared some weeks ago in the Winnipeg Tribune. The cartoon shows the wall of Lower Fort Garry down the Red River from the city of Winnipeg. There is a Canadian flag flying from it. Standing on guard in a uniform of some decades ago is an officer. Across his chest are the words "Judd Buchanan".

subtopic: ADMISSION FEES TO LOWER FORT GARRY-RIDEAU CANAL TOLLS-TERRA NOVA PARK TRAVEL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ADMISSION FEES TO LOWER FORT GARRY-RIDEAU CANAL TOLLS-TERRA NOVA PARK TRAVEL
speechtext: On his officer's cap there is a dollar sign.

subtopic: ADMISSION FEES TO LOWER FORT GARRY-RIDEAU CANAL TOLLS-TERRA NOVA PARK TRAVEL
speechtext: How many?

subtopic: ADMISSION FEES TO LOWER FORT GARRY-RIDEAU CANAL TOLLS-TERRA NOVA PARK TRAVEL
speechtext:
There is only one dollar sign, but it stands for quite a few dollars. The caption on the cartoon reads as follows: "Let's all salute history! That will be two bucks, please!"
My grievance with respect to the fee or fees being charged for admission to Lower Fort Garry was underlined this afternoon when the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mrs. Campagnolo) gave an oral answer to my question No. 2,486, which has been on the order paper since May 16.
The question had several parts to it having to do with when the Government of Canada became the owner of Lower Fort Garry, and so on. In particular, I asked from whom the Government of Canada obtained the property known as Lower Fort Garry. The answer was that it was obtained from the Hudson's Bay Company. I asked how much the Hudson's Bay Company charged the Government of Canada for the acres that comprise Lower Fort Garry. The figures vary. There is a $2 fee for a single admission for any person who is 16 years of age or over. There is a 50 cent fee for persons below that age. There is a $10 annual fee. subtopic: BILINGUALISM-POSSIBLE REFERENCE OF QUEBEC'S BILL 22 TO SUPREME COURT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BILINGUALISM-POSSIBLE REFERENCE OF QUEBEC'S BILL 22 TO SUPREME COURT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on May 9 last I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) some questions. One was this: had he received the brief of the Quebec Association of Protestant School Boards and others dealing with Bill 22, the Quebec Official Language Act, and would he refer it to the Supreme Court of Canada? Secondly, how could he, who is supposed to be so committed to bilingualism, continue to ignore a bill so committed to a contrary view? He said he would not refer it, and then he tried to slide out of his dilemma by saying that he had no jurisdiction to do so, that his government only had jurisdiction with respect to areas under the authority of the federal government.
Such an answer is patent constitutional nonsense, and one cannot be more direct than that. If he meant that it
6500

June 5, 1975
Adjournment Motion
was clear that Bill 22 did not encroach into the federal jurisdiction, then with respect he is equally wrong.
I want to draw your attention to a few sections of that bill. Section 1, which makes French the sole official language of Quebec, violates section 133 of the British North America Act, which makes both French and English official languages in Quebec for the legislature and courts. Section 2, which makes the French text of Quebec laws prevail over the English text in case of conflict, also violates section 133 of the British North America Act.
The sections dealing with the language of instruction in education violate section 93 of the BNA Act, which prohibits any provincial law that "prejudicially affects any right or privilege with respect to denominational education which any class of person had by law in the province" at confederation. All Quebec public schools are denominational. Pre-confederation provincial acts vested the "management and control" of denominational schools and the right to "choose the language of instruction" and to "regulate the course of study" in the denominational school boards. This right, therefore, the province cannot take away. Eleven other sections, in so far as they apply to schools, also violate section 93 of the British North America Act.
The sections dealing with the language of communications with other governments of Canada, language of labour relations, and language of business contracts, are unconstitutional in so far as they purport to apply to the federal government or its institutions, or to any other employers covered by the federal Official Languages Act, or to interprovincial trade and commerce.
The sections dealing with the language of public utilities are unconstitutional in so far as they purport to apply to interprovincial telephone, telegraph, air, ship, railway, gas pipeline and autobus operations, since all such operations come under exclusive federal jurisdiction.
The sections requiring the use of French in company names are unconstitutional in so far as they purport to apply to federally incorporated companies.
The section requiring the use of French labels on products is unconstitutional in so far as food and drugs are concerned, because it conflicts with the federal Food and Drugs Act. It is also unconstitutional in so far as it purports to control the import or export of products without French labels, or their sale.
The sections requiring the use of French in advertising and public signs are unconstitutional in so far as they purport to apply to television, and to interprovincial and international trade and commerce, which are under exclusively federal jurisdiction.
The next question that arises is whether the government ought to disallow the bill. The national interest calls for the promotion of our two principal cultures, French and English, on a basis of equality. This is accepted by all federal political parties. The Official Languages Act of Quebec undermines the whole concept of two equal cultures, and employs coercive measures to impose the French language on, and government control over, some of the chief institutions of English culture in the province.
English is the language most often spoken in the home by some 900,000 Quebecers, and by some 700,000 in met-

ropolitan Montreal alone. Quebec is the fourth largest English-speaking province, and Montreal the third largest English-speaking city, in Canada. Of the 112 provincial acts disallowed since confederation, 32 have been disallowed partly because they were considered contrary to the public interest of Canada as a whole.
Second, the act is contrary to constitutional principles and sound principles of legislation. It reaches down into the minutest details of daily life, as none of the legislation designed to limit the use of French in other provinces in the past has ever done. It vests in the provincial government and its agencies an unparalleled degree of discretionary power, and makes their decisions, in many vital matters, absolute and uncontrollable, denying to the citizen recourse to the courts.
Third, the act is contrary to reason, justice, and natural equity, a ground given for disallowing five acts of other provinces.
Fourth, it is contrary to federal policy as set forth in the federal Official Languages Act. Fourteen provincial acts have been disallowed partly for this reason.
Fifth, it is discriminatory. It discriminates against members of the professions who do not have what the provincial government considers an adequate knowledge of French; against business firms which, in the opinion of the provincial government, have not "francisized" themselves; against the English language universities. Its educational sections discriminate against the ethnic groups, and against French Canadians who may wish to send their children to English language schools. Fourteen acts have been disallowed partly because they are discriminatory. Ten acts have been disallowed because of the vagueness of their terms, and this bill is certainly vague. Madam Speaker, this is a burning ember in the fabric of our national unity, and for that reason alone this bill ought to be referred or disallowed.

subtopic: HEALTH-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION NOT TO TEST FOR MERCURY POISONING AMONG NATIVES
HEALTH-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION NOT TO TEST FOR MERCURY POISONING AMONG NATIVES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have asked for this time to clarify for myself and for many other people who are involved just exactly what the position of the government is in relation to the question of arsenic and mercury pollution in Yellowknife.
Several times in press releases and in speeches the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has indicated that the survey results released last week by his department represented only a part of the testing program. He said, as reported at page 6379 of Hansard, that "more thorough studies have been launched, particularly on established cases showing what appears to be a high arsenic rate."
The only source the government has of finding high arsenic rates is its own study, and frankly I find that study suspect. The difficulty lies with the sample on which that study is based. I believe 700 people volunteered for the survey. Roughly speaking, less than 20 per cent of the samples were from mine and mill workers, and only 8 per cent were from native people. By my calculation that means only 28 per cent of the samples were from people most directly connected with arsenic.
It is the workers, for obvious reasons, and the native people who are most directly connected with arsenic
Adjournment Motion
because many of them have been using Back Bay in Yellowknife as their source of drinking water, and Back Bay is polluted with arsenic and mercury. The point I am trying to make, Madam Speaker, is that if the minister is going to base his next round of tests on his first study, then he is going to miss a lot of people who potentially have high readings of arsenic in their bodies.
Let me illustrate this with an example. You have heard mention of a study commissioned by the Indian Brotherhood. The testing for this survey was conducted by the University of Toronto. Their sample is suspect because it only contained 18 individuals. However, they did find two children with mercury readings. One had a reading of 180, the other of 90.
The minister's study also found some examples of mercury, but they were very low. Let me quote from a department press release dated May 27:
Since the presently accepted maximum safety level for mercury is 60 parts per million it is not considered necessary to do any follow-up studies on the mercury levels at this time.
One of the two children I mentioned had a reading three times what the minister's department calls the maximum safety level. Because his first survey was not relevant to the matter at hand, his department missed this one example. And because they missed the one example, they are not going to test for mercury.
My worry is for the other ten year olds and their families whom the minister's survey did not find, and I think that the life and health of these people are worth any effort the minister might have made to design and carry out a survey that will give a more accurate picture of the situation in Yellowknife. Armed with relevant data, he should then proceed with further studies.
The second point I would like the minister to take to heart concerns the attitude of some of his staff, and the staff of other departments, when they are dealing with the public in these matters.
As I remember it, .last January when the CBC made public the allegedly secret document which revealed the levels of arsenic present in the environment of Yellowknife, a great number of attacks and counter-attacks were made about whether the document was indeed secret. The upshot of the whole thing was the announcement of the survey that came out last week, and what appeared to be a pledge that every pertinent fact on the subject of arsenic would be made available to the public.
I have a memo, dated February 6-a time when the commotion had died down somewhat. It is from Mr. H. Veldhuizen of the air pollution control section of the Environmental Protection Service. It went to Mr. C. A. Lewis of the EPS in Yellowknife. Copies went to Dr. R. D. P. Eaton in Edmonton, who is an employee of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
It deals with the recommendation of a body in the United States charged with evaluating standards for health in working environments. It seems that this body now recommends that the industrial hygiene standards for in-plant environmental conditions be lowered from 500 micrograms per cubic metre to 4 micrograms per cubic metre. Mr. Veldhuizen explains this change to Mr. Lewis in some detail. Then he says:
295 61 - 6714

June 5, 1975
Adjournment Motion
It would be advisable not to release this information to the public as it may cause undue concern at this time.
I would like to ask the minister to justify that kind of attitude in a person hired with public money to protect the public.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION NOT TO TEST FOR MERCURY POISONING AMONG NATIVES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in response to the question of the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) put to the minister this afternoon on the National Indian Brotherhood survey, I would like to say the following.
During the survey on arsenic levels in hair samples of residents of the Yellowknife area which was carried out in February of 1975 by the department, tests for mercury were also done on 20 per cent of the hair samples. These tests were done because a study carried out by researchers of the University of Iowa some time ago had indicated the possibility of mercury contamination also occurring as a result of the processing of gold ore at Yellowknife. The study of arsenic levels provided an opportunity to obtain up to date information on the possibility of a mercury problem, since the presence of mercury in human hair is a good indication of whether, and to what extent, it is present in the body.
All the hair samples tested for mercury revealed levels of less than 10 parts per million (ppm) with one exception, which was 25 ppm. Since the presently accepted maximum safety level for mercury is 60 ppm, it was concluded that further follow up studies on mercury levels were not necessary at that time. This conclusion was the one made known in the press release of May 27, 1975.
Since that time officials of the National Indian Brotherhood have contacted officials of the department to inform them of the results of a survey carried out for the NIB on arsenic and mercury levels in some hair samples of residents of two native communities very near Yellowknife. As reported to the department, this survey was of 18 hair samples, but levels of mercury were reported on only two of the samples. Both of these samples are reported to have revealed significantly elevated levels of mercury.
When told of these results, the department immediately requested the National Indian Brotherhood to provide it with a full report on the survey because it wished to follow up with further tests on any individuals found by the NIB to have significant arsenic or mercury hair levels. We have not yet received the report from NIB, and are therefore not yet able to draw any conclusions about the two mercury levels reported, or on the methodology used in the tests.
In the meantime, however, the results reported by NIB have already been reported to the northern health services with the instructions that they are to contact the individuals concerned and ask them to have clinical examinations during phase II of the Yellowknife survey which will start on June 9.
Whether still further tests or surveys should be conducted at this time in connection with mercury is something which will be assessed when the department has had an opportunity to study the full report of the NIB survey and these clinical examinations have been done. The fact remains that the much larger survey carried out by the

department did not reveal any mercury levels of significance, and the two high levels reported from the NIB survey must be examined in that light.
Despite this fact, I want to assure the hon. member and the House that in addition to the immediate steps I have described, the department will follow up with whatever further work we find to be necessary to monitor the health of the residents in the area and to enable us to take measures to protect it.

subtopic: FINANCE-EXCISE TAX ON PRIVATE AIRCRAFT AND PLEASURE BOATS-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS IN LIMITING CONSUMPTION OF PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
FINANCE-EXCISE TAX ON PRIVATE AIRCRAFT AND PLEASURE BOATS-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS IN LIMITING CONSUMPTION OF PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in Hansard for May 30 at page 6280 is recorded the question I asked of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), as follows:
With respect to the 10 per cent excise tax on privately owned aircraft and motor driven pleasure boats, which was part of the November budget, will the minister now advise as to what degree this tax has limited oil consumption in Canada?
The Minister of Finance replied:
-I will have to consult with my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, but I would hope it had some result.
On January 9 I wrote to the Minister of Finance, and I quote from that letter:
Regarding the 10% tax on non-commercial aircraft and pleasure boats I am forced to ask whether anyone really believes this is the way to cut down on the consumption of oil. Surely this move is unnecessary and, for that matter, not based on any real programme for energy conservation. Ration gas, tax gas, or let the price rise, if you really want to cut down on consumption, but why try and pretend that this tax is going to help to maintain Canadian self-sufficiency in energy?
On February 19 the Minister of Finance replied, and wrote the following:
The special excise taxes on energy-consuming vehicles constitute one of several programs the government has introduced to deal with the critical question of conserving Canada's energy resources.
In the following paragraph it is stated that:
... the government is aware that the impact of the new taxes on industries directly affected will result in some short-term dislocations in those industries. However, it must be emphasized that disruptions in industries directly related to the consumption of petroleum products will inevitably occur, and the government must take action now to encourage such industries and consumers to adjust their production and consumption in the direction of more conservative energy-consuming products if even greater dislocations are to be avoided.
I want to say quite frankly that if that is the result of this tax, then of course the public must have some sympathy with it, but I wish to record tonight my own severe doubts that that tax has had any effect on the consumption of oil in Canada.
I want to quote from some letters which I have received, as a member of parliament, from people operating in the marine industry in my own province. I quote from a letter dated May 12, 1975, from Leo Edwards Sons, Ltd. as follows:
The imposition of the tax has resulted in decreased sales, lay-offs and has contributed to inflation rather than otherwise.
June 5, 1975

The letter also says:
I would like to point out that less than Vi of 1 per cent of the total fuel used in Canada is used for boating.
I have a copy of a letter sent to the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Raines), a member on the government side, on April 16, 1975, by Taylor Pearson & Carson (B.C.). It reads in part:
We feel that the discriminatory additional 10 per cent tax is having a bad effect on the profitability of our independent marine dealers in British Columbia.
I should also like to quote from a letter from Capstan Marine of Richmond, British Columbia, dated May 14, 1975, as follows:
This new policy has been very detrimental to the marine industry. The excise tax is not the type of lavement our industry needed.
May I quote again, this time from a letter dated April 29, 1975, from Allied Boating-Canada which is located in Ontario. The letter reads in part:
It is estimated that gasoline sold through retail outlets in Canada is well in excess of five billion gallons (no penalty).
It is estimated that gasoline for the use of snowmobiles in Canada is 57 million gallons (no penalty).
It is estimated that gasoline sold for the use of small boats in Canada is 77 million gallons (penalized).
When you add in industrial, farm, aircraft and heating fuels, it is estimated that the small boat consumption of fuel is less than '/j of 1 per cent of the Canadian fuel consumption.
This can hardly be classed as an area of high energy consumption!
A letter dated May 14 from Simpson Power Products, Ltd. reads as follows:
The subject tax has now been in effect for approximately six months, and, from our company's own experience, if your goal was to kill the pleasure boat industry in Canada, you have succeeded 100 per cent.
We know this was not your intention. You stated it was a fuel conservation measure, but you chose to pick on an industry that is the smallest in the luxury market, and, due to competition from the large mass producers in the U.S.A., has always had a struggle to keep out of the red.
I want to say to the minister that there are plenty more letters along these lines. I hope the minister can satisfy us tonight that this tax has had a degree of success in conservation of the total amount of oil consumed in Canada. If that were so then I would say to all hon. members and to the public that we have to look upon it sympathetically.
I put on the record as early as January, Madam Speaker, that I doubted the real conservation effects of this tax. I ask the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cullen) to tell us tonight whether the tax
Adjournment Motion
has had any appreciable effect on reducing the consumption of oil based fuels in this country. I ask him also to tell us exactly the amount of that reduction, and if the figures are not available I would ask him to give an estimate.
Unless it has some significance this tax is not only foolish, it is clearly discriminatory against owners of boats and airplanes in relation to a great many other users of gasoline products in this country. There is no justification whatsoever for visiting a tax on one particular industry unless it has a very significant effect in terms of conservation. Unless it can be clearly justified, this is a discriminatory tax and ought to be removed in the coming budget.

In addition, the government has made significant changes in taxation of the petroleum industries, and a phased reduction in the exports of oil has been initiated.

The combined effect of these measures has been to indicate to industries and consumers the urgent need to adjust production and consumption in the direction of products which consume less energy. Although the excise taxes referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) constitute a modest step in this direction, the effect of these taxes has been to make both consumers and producers more conscious of the need to conserve energy.
It is difficult to isolate the precise effects of these special excise taxes. The government is satisfied that its over-all policies to encourage energy conservation will have the desired results. I should like to assure the hon. member for Vancouver South that the government will continue to monitor developments in the field of energy conservation very carefully.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.29 p.m.
